choices: It is generative AI because it is a chatbot, so an agent is the natural next step
It is computer vision because it detects objects, so a read-only classifier is enough
It is information extraction because it saves invoice fields, so an agent should store them
It is text analysis using named entity detection, and an agent would add cost and risk the task does not need
questions.why: The bot interprets existing text and labels named entities without creating content or acting, so it is text analysis, and mislabeling it could lead to an unsupervised agent where a read-only classifier is enough.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which AI workload category a business scenario belongs to. Include one case where two categories overlap and say how you would choose between them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I look at what goes in, what comes out, and whether the system creates something or takes action. If it writes new text or images from a prompt, it's generative AI. If it plans steps and uses tools to act, like approving a refund, it's agentic AI. If it labels existing text by tone, entities, key phrases or summary, it's text analysis. Audio to text or text to audio is speech. Understanding photos or video is computer vision. Pulling named fields out of documents or recordings is information extraction. The categories overlap. Reading a scanned invoice uses vision, but if the goal is the invoice number and total in a database, I call it information extraction, because I label by the main goal. There is a tradeoff: picking an agent when a simple classifier would do adds cost and the risk of unsupervised actions.
rubricPoints: Classifies by input, output, and whether the system creates or acts.
Distinguishes generative AI (creates content) from agentic AI (plans and takes actions with tools).
Correctly describes text analysis, speech, computer vision, and information extraction.
Names an overlap, such as vision versus information extraction, and resolves it by the primary goal.
Notes a consequence of mislabelling, such as extra cost or the risk of unneeded autonomous actions.

suggested.rationale: This objective is tested by matching short business scenarios to a workload category, so reasoning through exam-style situations is the most useful practice, and no current mission or planned engine covers AI workloads.

lessons.plain: Text analysis is software reading written words and pulling useful facts out of them, so people do not have to read every message themselves. Four common jobs are listing the main talking points (keyword extraction), spotting named things like people, places, companies and dates (entity detection), judging whether the writer sounds happy, unhappy or neutral (sentiment analysis), and boiling a long text down to a short version (summarization). Picture a sharp assistant with a stack of customer letters and four highlighters. One marks topics, one marks names, one marks mood, and one writes a two-line recap for the boss.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company receives thousands of product reviews a day and wants to flag the angry ones quickly. Which of these four jobs would you reach for: listing topics, finding names, judging mood, or shortening the text?
lessons.teach:
Text analysis means using natural language processing (NLP), the branch of AI that lets software work with human language, to turn unstructured text such as reviews, emails or support tickets into structured facts. Four techniques come up most.

Keyword extraction (Azure calls it key phrase extraction) returns the main talking points of a passage as short phrases. Entity detection, also called named entity recognition, finds specific real-world things and labels each one with a category such as person, location, organization, date or quantity. Some services also do entity linking, which ties a mention to a reference entry so that Paris the city is told apart from a person named Paris. Sentiment analysis rates emotional tone as positive, negative, neutral or mixed. It gives a confidence score for each rating, a number from 0 to 1 showing how sure the model is, and it scores each sentence as well as the whole document. Summarization shortens a document. Extractive summarization picks the most important original sentences. Abstractive summarization writes new sentences that capture the meaning.

These work because models trained on huge amounts of text learn patterns. They learn which words carry meaning, which word shapes signal names or dates, and which phrasing signals praise or complaint. In Microsoft Foundry, these come as Azure AI Language, a prebuilt managed service you call without training your own model.

Worked example. A review reads: "Stayed at the Harbor Inn in Seattle on 3 May. The room was spotless, but check-in took an hour." Step 1, key phrases: Harbor Inn, room, check-in. Step 2, entities: Harbor Inn (organization), Seattle (location), 3 May (date). Step 3, sentiment: sentence one neutral, sentence two mixed, overall mixed. Step 4, abstractive summary: "Clean room, slow check-in."

A common mistake is treating key phrases and entities as the same thing. A key phrase says what the text is about, such as check-in. An entity is a specific, categorised thing, such as Seattle as a location. A request to find every company name and date needs entity detection, not keyword extraction. In a running system, picking the wrong technique gives a complaint-routing dashboard vague topics instead of product names. Reading only the overall sentiment can also hide a serious complaint inside a mostly positive message.

questions.prompt: A parcel delivery company wants to send any customer message containing a complaint to its escalations team, even when the message is mostly friendly. A sample message reads: "Your drivers are always polite and quick. Today my parcel was left in the rain and the laptop inside is ruined. Thanks for the usual great service." Step 1: send each message to sentiment analysis. Step 2: the service returns an overall label (here, positive) plus a label and a confidence score (a number from 0 to 1 showing how sure the model is) for each sentence. Step 3: ??? Step 4: send every flagged message to the escalations queue. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Flag the message if the overall confidence score is below 0.5, because a low confidence score means the customer is unhappy.
Flag the message only if its overall label is negative, because the overall label already accounts for every sentence.
Run key phrase extraction and flag the message if it contains the phrase "complaint", because key phrases show emotional tone.
Check each sentence's label and flag the message if any sentence is rated negative, even though the overall label is positive.
questions.why: Sentiment analysis scores each sentence as well as the whole message, so checking the sentence-level labels catches the ruined-laptop complaint that a positive overall label would hide.

questions.prompt: A law firm wants software to scan thousands of contracts and list every client name, every city mentioned, and every signing date, with each item tagged by its category. Which text analysis technique fits this request?
choices: Entity detection (named entity recognition)
Extractive summarization
Sentiment analysis
Key phrase extraction
questions.why: Entity detection finds specific real-world things and labels each one with a category such as person, location or date, which is exactly what the firm needs.

questions.prompt: A hospital's records team needs short summaries of long incident reports. Their rule is that every sentence in a summary must appear word for word in the original report, so nothing is reworded. Which approach meets this rule?
choices: Sentiment analysis, because it scores each sentence separately
Key phrase extraction, because it returns the main talking points as short phrases
Extractive summarization, because it picks the most important original sentences
Abstractive summarization, because it writes new sentences that capture the meaning
questions.why: Extractive summarization keeps the original sentences unchanged, while abstractive summarization writes new wording, which would break the team's rule.

questions.prompt: A phone retailer builds a dashboard meant to show which competitor companies customers mention in reviews. The developers used key phrase extraction, and the dashboard now shows items like "battery life" and "delivery delay" instead of company names. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The reviews must first be summarized with abstractive summarization before company names can be found
Key phrase extraction returns the main talking points, not categorised real-world things; finding company names needs entity detection
The confidence scores were too low, so company names were filtered out
Key phrase extraction only works on positive reviews, so negative reviews lost their company names
questions.why: Key phrases say what text is about, while entity detection labels specific things such as organizations, so picking the wrong technique produced vague topics instead of company names.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how keyword extraction, entity detection, sentiment analysis and summarization differ, using one customer email as your example, and name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: All four are NLP techniques that turn free text into something structured, but each answers a different question. Keyword extraction answers "what is this about?" by returning key phrases like "late delivery" or "refund". Entity detection answers "which specific things are named?" and labels them by category, such as the order date, the city and the courier company. Sentiment analysis answers "how does the writer feel?" with positive, negative, neutral or mixed, plus a confidence score per sentence and overall. Summarization answers "what is the short version?" either by picking key original sentences (extractive) or by writing new ones (abstractive). One limit is that overall sentiment can average away a single furious sentence, so check sentence-level scores for complaints. Abstractive summaries read well but can phrase things the writer never said, so extractive is safer when exact wording matters.
rubricPoints: Identifies keyword extraction as returning the main topics or phrases of a text.
Identifies entity detection as finding specific named things and labelling them with categories like person, place, organization or date.
Describes sentiment analysis as rating tone as positive, negative, neutral or mixed with a confidence score.
Distinguishes extractive summarization (original sentences) from abstractive summarization (newly written sentences).
Names a real limit, such as overall sentiment hiding a negative sentence or abstractive summaries drifting from the source.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine performs text analysis, and the exam skill is matching a business scenario to the right technique, so reasoning through scenario-style questions helps most.

lessons.plain: Speech recognition and speech synthesis are two opposite directions of the same job. Speech recognition, also called speech-to-text, listens to spoken audio and writes down the words as text. Speech synthesis, also called text-to-speech, takes written text and reads it aloud in a computer-generated voice. Think of a court stenographer who types everything said in a room, and an audiobook narrator who turns a printed page into sound. A voice assistant uses both. It transcribes what you say, works out a reply, and then speaks that reply back to you. On Azure these capabilities are offered by a managed speech service.
lessons.guessPrompt: A museum wants visitors to hear an exhibit's written description played aloud through headphones. Which direction is that: turning speech into text, or turning text into speech?
lessons.teach:
Speech recognition (speech-to-text) converts spoken audio into written text. Speech synthesis (text-to-speech) converts written text into spoken audio. On Azure both come from Azure AI Speech, a managed speech service you can reach through Microsoft Foundry, which is Microsoft's platform for building AI apps.

Recognition works by combining two kinds of model. An acoustic model maps slices of sound to phonemes, which are the smallest units of speech sound. A language model predicts which word sequences are likely, so that "recognize speech" wins over "wreck a nice beach". Useful recognition features include real-time transcription, which produces live text as someone talks, for example in captions. Batch transcription processes recorded files later. Custom speech means training on your own vocabulary, such as product names or medical terms. Speaker diarization labels which speaker said each part of a conversation.

Synthesis uses neural voices, which are voices generated by deep learning models trained on recorded human speech, so they sound natural. You choose a voice and language. You can fine-tune delivery with SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language), a markup format that controls speaking rate, pitch, pauses and pronunciation. Custom voice creates a voice unique to a brand. Speech translation combines recognition with translation into another language.

Worked example, a phone helpline. First, the caller says "I need to reset my password." Second, recognition turns that audio into the text string. Third, the application decides on a reply as text. Fourth, synthesis speaks the reply in a neural voice, with an SSML pause before the reset code is read out.

Common mistake: assuming speech recognition understands meaning or identifies the person. It only produces words. Working out intent is language understanding, and verifying identity is speaker recognition, which are separate capabilities. In a running system, skipping custom speech for jargon-heavy audio causes misheard terms, which then flow downstream as wrong text and lead to wrong actions.

questions.prompt: A podcast network wants searchable text for its back catalogue. Every episode features two hosts and one guest. Step 1: the network uploads 300 recorded episodes and lets them process overnight, so it uses batch transcription rather than live captions. Step 2: the hosts often mention sponsor product names that standard models mishear, so the team trains custom speech on a list of those names. Step 3 (missing): the transcript must show which of the three people said each line. Step 4: editors search the labelled text to pull guest quotes. Which capability completes Step 3?
choices: Speaker recognition, to verify each person's identity
Speaker diarization, to label who spoke each part
Custom voice, to give each person a unique voice
Real-time transcription, to produce live text
questions.why: Speaker diarization labels which speaker said each part of a conversation, which is exactly what Step 3 needs, whereas speaker recognition verifies identity and custom voice is a synthesis feature.

questions.prompt: A city transit authority uses text-to-speech for platform announcements. Passengers complain that the platform number is read too quickly to catch. Which feature lets the team add a pause and slow the speaking rate just before the number?
choices: Batch transcription
Custom speech
Speaker diarization
SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language)
questions.why: SSML is the markup format that controls speaking rate, pitch, pauses and pronunciation in synthesized speech.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic transcribes vets' spoken notes into text. Drug names such as unusual animal medications keep coming out as wrong everyday words, and the wrong text is then copied into treatment records. What is the most suitable fix?
choices: Use speech translation into another language
Train custom speech on the clinic's drug vocabulary
Switch to a different neural voice
Add speaker diarization to the transcripts
questions.why: Custom speech trains recognition on your own vocabulary, so specialist terms are not misheard and passed downstream as wrong text.

questions.prompt: A bank's phone system already uses speech recognition to turn callers' words into text. A manager says this means the system can also confirm that the caller really is the account holder. Why is the manager wrong?
choices: Speech recognition only produces words; verifying identity is speaker recognition
Speech recognition only works on recorded files, not live calls
Speech recognition identifies people but only after custom voice is trained
Identity checks require SSML, which the bank has not added
questions.why: Speech recognition just converts audio to text; verifying who is speaking is a separate capability called speaker recognition.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between speech recognition and speech synthesis, give one feature of each, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Speech recognition, or speech-to-text, turns audio into written words. Speech synthesis, or text-to-speech, does the reverse and reads text aloud. On Azure both come from the Azure AI Speech service. On the recognition side, we can transcribe live for captions or in batch for recorded files. Diarization tells us who spoke when, and custom speech teaches the model our product names. On the synthesis side, we pick a natural-sounding neural voice and use SSML to control speed, pitch, pauses and pronunciation. The limit is that recognition only gives us words. It doesn't understand intent or confirm who the speaker is, so we need other capabilities for that. Accuracy also drops with noisy audio or specialist jargon unless we invest in a custom model. That costs effort to train and keep up to date.
rubricPoints: Speech recognition converts audio to text and speech synthesis converts text to audio.
Names at least one recognition feature such as real-time or batch transcription, diarization or custom speech.
Names at least one synthesis feature such as neural voices, SSML or custom voice.
States that recognition produces words but does not understand intent or identify the speaker.
Notes an accuracy tradeoff such as noise or jargon, needing custom models.

suggested.rationale: The unit is about matching scenarios to the right capability, so reasoning through exam-style cases such as captions, voice assistants and narration is the best practice, and no current mission or planned engine covers speech.

lessons.plain: Computer vision is the part of AI that lets software make sense of pictures and video: saying what an image shows, finding and counting objects in it, reading printed or handwritten text, or writing a sentence that describes it. Image generation runs the other way. You describe a picture in words, and a model creates a new image that matches. Think of a museum guide and a sketch artist. The guide looks at a painting and tells you what is in it. The artist listens to your description and draws something new. Vision models are the guide, and image-generation models are the artist.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants software to count how many cereal boxes are on each shelf from a photo. Would an AI that only answers 'this photo contains cereal boxes' be enough? If not, what extra information would it need to give?
lessons.teach:
Computer vision models take an image as input and return information about it. These are the main capabilities. Image classification gives one label, or a few labels, for the whole image, such as 'dog' or 'damaged part'. Object detection finds each separate object and returns a label, a bounding box (a rectangle marking where the object sits), and a confidence score (how sure the model is, from 0 to 1). Semantic segmentation labels every pixel, so you get the exact outline of each object instead of a rough rectangle. Optical character recognition (OCR) reads printed or handwritten text in the image. Image tagging and captioning return keywords or a plain-language sentence describing the scene. Face detection finds where faces are, which is not the same as identifying who a person is.

These work because the model was trained on many labelled images. During training it learned patterns of edges, shapes and textures that go with each label.

Image-generation models go in the opposite direction. They take a text prompt (your written description) and produce a new image. Many of them are diffusion models. A diffusion model starts from random noise and removes a little of it at each step, steering every step toward the prompt until a clear picture appears. Some newer multimodal models (models that handle more than one kind of input, such as text and images) can both describe images and create them. In Microsoft Foundry you can choose prebuilt vision services or deploy such models.

Worked example: a street photo. Classification returns 'street scene'. Detection returns car (0.97), car (0.94) and person (0.91), each with a box, which gives a count of two cars. OCR reads a sign saying 'Main St'. Captioning returns 'A person crosses a busy street'.

A common mistake is to pick classification when the task needs counting or locating things. Classification only says what the image contains. It does not say how many objects there are or where they are. A shelf-audit system built on classification would never report empty spaces or counts.

questions.prompt: A fruit grower flies a drone over an orchard and sends one photo to a vision model. Here is how each need maps to a capability. Step 1: the grower wants one overall label for the photo, so image classification returns 'apple orchard'. Step 2: the grower wants a count of ripe apples on one branch, so object detection returns apple (0.92), apple (0.88), apple (0.85) and apple (0.81), each with a bounding box, which gives a count of four. Step 3: the grower wants to read the batch number painted on a wooden crate, so OCR returns 'Batch 14'. Step 4 is missing: the grower wants the exact outline of the bruised patch on one apple, pixel by pixel, not a rough rectangle. Which capability fills Step 4?
choices: Image captioning, because it describes the bruise in a sentence
Semantic segmentation, because it labels every pixel and gives the exact outline
Image classification, because it labels the photo as 'bruised'
Object detection, because it returns a bounding box around the bruise
questions.why: Only semantic segmentation labels each pixel, so it traces the precise shape of the bruise instead of drawing a rectangle around it or labelling the whole image.

questions.prompt: A museum wants its gallery cameras to blur visitors' faces before footage is stored. The system only needs to know where faces appear in each frame, not who the visitors are. Which computer vision capability fits this need?
choices: Image classification, which gives the whole frame one label
Optical character recognition, which reads text in the frame
Face detection, which finds where faces are without identifying anyone
Image captioning, which writes a sentence describing the scene
questions.why: Face detection locates faces in an image, which is all that is needed to blur them, and it is different from identifying who a person is.

questions.prompt: A bakery photographs each tray, which should hold 12 muffins, and runs an image classification model on the photo. The model keeps returning 'muffin tray' even when three muffins are missing. What is the best fix?
choices: Retrain the classification model with more photos of full trays
Raise the confidence score threshold on the classification label
Switch to object detection so each muffin gets a box and the system can count them
Use image captioning so the model writes 'a tray of muffins'
questions.why: Classification only says what the image contains, not how many objects there are or where they sit, whereas object detection returns one box per muffin, which allows counting.

questions.prompt: A marketing team types the prompt 'a red bicycle leaning on a blue door' into a diffusion-based image-generation model. How does the model produce the picture?
choices: It searches a library of stock photos and returns the closest match to the prompt
It runs object detection on the prompt text and draws a bounding box for each object
It classifies the prompt into one label and then copies a training image with that label
It starts from random noise and removes a little at each step, steering each step toward the prompt
questions.why: A diffusion model begins with random noise and gradually removes it over many steps, guiding each step toward the text prompt until a clear new image appears.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between image classification, object detection, OCR and image generation. Use a scenario to show which one fits. Name one limit, for example what classification cannot tell you, or why generated images need checking.
lessons.modelAnswer: Vision models analyse an existing image, while image-generation models create a new one. Classification gives a label for the whole picture, such as 'contains a cat'. Object detection goes further and finds each object with a bounding box and a confidence score, so it is what you need for counting or locating things. For counting stock on shelves, detection fits and classification does not, because classification can't tell you how many items there are or where they are. OCR reads text in an image, such as the label on a parcel. Captioning describes the scene in a sentence. Image generation, often done with a diffusion model, turns a text prompt into a new picture by refining random noise step by step. One limit is that both kinds of model can be wrong. Detection gives confidence scores rather than certainty, and a generated image may not match the prompt exactly, so a person should review the output.
rubricPoints: Separates analysing an existing image (vision) from creating a new image (generation).
States that classification labels the whole image, while detection returns each object with a location box and a confidence score.
Identifies OCR as reading text and captioning as describing the scene.
Describes image generation as producing an image from a text prompt, for example by a diffusion model refining noise.
Matches a capability to a concrete scenario, such as counting needing detection.
Names a limit, such as classification having no counts or positions, or outputs being uncertain.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is reading a scenario and naming the vision capability it needs, so working through short situations teaches this best, and no current mission or planned engine covers computer vision.

lessons.plain: Information extraction means pulling specific, useful facts out of messy content and turning them into tidy, labelled data a program can use. The content might be text (an email), an image (a photo of a receipt), audio (a recorded phone call) or video (a training clip). The output is a set of named fields, such as invoice number, total, or the date a caller mentioned. Think of a clerk who reads a stack of paper forms and types each answer into the right box of a spreadsheet. The AI does the reading and the box-filling, so people only check the answers it is unsure about.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company scans thousands of paper invoices as photos. If a computer can already turn the picture into plain text, what extra work is still needed before the company's accounting system can automatically record the total owed and the due date?
lessons.teach:
Information extraction is the AI workload that converts unstructured content into structured data: named fields with values, often with a confidence score. Unstructured means there is no fixed layout a program can rely on. Structured means organised into predictable fields, like columns in a table or keys in a record.

Each kind of input needs a first step that turns it into something readable. For images and scanned documents, optical character recognition (OCR) detects printed or handwritten characters and outputs text with positions. Layout analysis then finds structure such as tables, paragraphs, checkboxes and key-value pairs (a label next to its answer, like 'Due date: 3 May'). For audio, speech-to-text transcription produces a written transcript, often with timestamps and labels for who spoke. For video, the system combines transcription of the soundtrack, OCR of on-screen text and analysis of frames to produce a time-indexed description. Once content is text plus structure, a field-extraction step maps it onto a schema: a list of the fields you want and their types. Prebuilt models cover common documents such as invoices, receipts and ID cards; custom models are trained or instructed for your own forms. In Microsoft Foundry, services such as Azure AI Document Intelligence and Azure AI Content Understanding provide these capabilities.

Worked example: a phone photo of an invoice arrives. OCR reads every word and its location. Layout analysis spots a table of line items and the pair 'Total: 412.50'. The invoice model maps that to the field InvoiceTotal = 412.50 with confidence 0.97, and DueDate = 2025-05-03 with confidence 0.61. The application records the total automatically and sends the due date to a person to confirm.

A common mistake is treating OCR or transcription as the whole job. Raw text is not yet data; without field extraction, someone still has to find the total by hand. Another mistake is ignoring confidence scores: a running system that accepts every value will silently write wrong amounts into accounts, so low-confidence fields should be routed to human review.

questions.prompt: A town council wants the decisions from its recorded meetings stored as data. The input is an audio file of a two-hour meeting with no video. The pipeline so far: Step 1 is MISSING. Step 2: a schema is defined with the fields MotionNumber (number), Outcome (passed or failed) and VotesFor (number). Step 3: field extraction maps the text onto that schema, giving MotionNumber = 17 with confidence 0.95, Outcome = passed with confidence 0.93, and VotesFor = 6 with confidence 0.58. Step 4: the application publishes the motion number and outcome automatically and sends VotesFor to the council clerk to check. What is Step 1?
choices: Run speech-to-text transcription to produce a written transcript, with timestamps and labels for who spoke
Apply a prebuilt invoice model directly to the audio, because it already knows how to find number fields
Run optical character recognition (OCR) on the audio file to detect the characters that were spoken
Run layout analysis on the recording to find the table of votes and the key-value pairs
questions.why: Audio must first become readable text through speech-to-text transcription before field extraction can map it onto the schema, while OCR and layout analysis work on images and documents, not sound.

questions.prompt: A climbing gym scans thousands of paper membership forms. Which of these is the kind of output that information extraction aims to produce?
choices: A record such as MemberName = 'R. Osei' (confidence 0.96) and EmergencyPhone = '0412 555 019' (confidence 0.88)
A clearer, higher-resolution image of each scanned form
A folder that groups the scanned forms by the month they were signed
One long block of all the words on each form, in reading order
questions.why: Information extraction turns unstructured content into structured data: named fields with values, often with a confidence score, while a block of raw text is not yet data.

questions.prompt: A university wants to search its recorded lectures for any moment where a topic is either spoken by the lecturer or shown on a slide. Which approach fits this information-extraction need?
choices: Speech-to-text transcription of the soundtrack alone, because slides add nothing a lecturer does not say
Layout analysis of the audio track to locate key-value pairs in the speech
OCR of the slides alone, because on-screen text is the only reliable source
Combine transcription of the soundtrack, OCR of on-screen text and analysis of frames into a time-indexed description
questions.why: For video, the system combines soundtrack transcription, OCR of on-screen text and frame analysis to produce a time-indexed description, which covers both what is said and what is shown.

questions.prompt: A delivery company extracts the field AmountCollected from scanned driver receipts. Its system writes every extracted value straight into customer accounts, including one of 840.00 with confidence 0.41. What is the main problem, and how should the system handle it?
choices: Confidence scores only matter for audio, so the value is fine to accept as it is
The amount is wrong because the schema lacks a type, so the field should be renamed
The confidence score shows OCR failed, so the receipt should be deleted and never processed
Low-confidence values are being accepted silently, so wrong amounts can enter accounts; such fields should be routed to a person for review
questions.why: A system that accepts every value regardless of confidence will silently record wrong amounts, so low-confidence fields should go to human review.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an AI system gets from a recorded customer call or a scanned form to usable data fields, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Information extraction turns unstructured content into structured fields a program can store. The first step depends on the input: OCR reads characters from images and scans, speech-to-text transcribes audio, and video combines transcription, on-screen OCR and frame analysis with timestamps. Layout analysis then finds structure like tables and key-value pairs. Finally, field extraction maps everything onto a schema, for example CustomerName, OrderNumber or InvoiceTotal, using a prebuilt model for common documents or a custom one for our own forms. Each value comes with a confidence score. The tradeoff is accuracy versus automation: poor scans, handwriting, background noise or accents lower confidence, so we should set a threshold and send uncertain fields to a human reviewer instead of trusting everything. That keeps errors out of downstream systems, but it costs reviewer time.
rubricPoints: Defines information extraction as turning unstructured content into structured, named fields.
Names the input-specific first step: OCR for images, transcription for audio, combined analysis for video.
Mentions mapping to a schema of fields, using prebuilt or custom models.
Notes that raw OCR text or a transcript alone is not yet usable data.
Identifies confidence scores and human review of low-confidence values as a limit or tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine exercises AI extraction, and the exam tests recognising which extraction technique fits a given scenario, which is best practised by reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: A generative AI model writes text in response to instructions. You usually give it two kinds of instruction. The system prompt is the standing briefing, set once by the app's builder: who the assistant is, what it may and may not do, and how answers should look. The user prompt is each individual request a person types. Think of a new hire at a help desk. The manager's briefing on day one is the system prompt. Each customer's question is a user prompt. Clear, specific instructions in both places get useful, consistent answers. Vague ones get guesses.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are building a cooking chatbot, and users keep getting long essays when they wanted a quick recipe. Would you fix this by asking every user to type 'be brief', or by changing something the app sends with every conversation? Why?
lessons.teach:
A system prompt is an instruction the application sends to a generative model at the start of every conversation. It sets the model's role, rules, tone and output format, and the end user normally never sees it. A user prompt is the message the person sends for one particular turn. The model reads both together and predicts a reply. In Microsoft Foundry, you can test both in the chat playground of a deployed model, and a client app sends them as messages with a 'system' role and a 'user' role.

Why does this work? The model has no other knowledge of your situation. Anything you leave unsaid, it fills in with a generic guess. Several techniques help. Give the model a role. State constraints, such as scope, length and what to do when it does not know. Specify the output format, such as a bulleted list or JSON. Add a few short examples of the input and the answer you want, which is called few-shot prompting. Supply relevant facts in the prompt, which is called grounding, so the model answers from your data rather than inventing details.

Here is a worked example. Version 1 has the system prompt 'You are helpful.' and the user prompt 'Tell me about returns.' The reply is a generic essay on retail returns. Version 2 keeps the same user prompt but changes the system prompt to: 'You are the support assistant for Contoso Outdoor. Answer only about Contoso orders. Our return window is 30 days with a receipt. Reply in at most three sentences. If unsure, say so and suggest contacting support.' Now the reply is short, accurate and on-brand.

A common mistake is putting lasting rules only in user prompts, or writing a vague system prompt and hoping. Behaviour then varies from turn to turn. In a running app, this shows up as inconsistent, off-topic or made-up answers. It also helps to remember that a system prompt guides the model but cannot guarantee obedience, so a determined user can sometimes talk it off course. Iterating on the prompt and testing it with realistic questions is part of the job.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam Recipes wants a deployed model in Microsoft Foundry to label each customer review of a recipe. The team builds the system prompt in steps. Step 1 (role): 'You are a review classifier for Fabrikam Recipes.' Step 2 (format): 'Reply only with JSON containing a field named sentiment, set to positive, negative or mixed.' They test this in the chat playground with 20 real reviews as user prompts. The labels come back inconsistent: some say 'kinda positive', and the same kind of review gets different labels on different turns. Step 3 is missing. Which change to the prompt most directly fixes this?
choices: Add three short sample reviews to the system prompt, each paired with the exact JSON answer wanted.
Paste the full Fabrikam recipe catalogue, with every ingredient list and cooking time, into the system prompt so the model has the facts it needs.
Add the sentence 'Be accurate and consistent' to the system prompt and change nothing else.
Leave the system prompt alone and repeat the JSON instruction at the start of every user prompt instead.
questions.why: Showing a few input-and-answer pairs (few-shot prompting) shows the model exactly what a correct label looks like, which makes its output consistent, whereas vague wording, rules moved into user prompts, or unrelated facts do not.

questions.prompt: An app for Tailwind Bank sends a deployed model two messages. The first message is hidden from the customer and reads: 'You are a savings advisor for Tailwind Bank. Never give tax advice. Keep replies under 100 words.' The second message is the customer's question: 'How do I open a savings account?' Which statement correctly describes these two messages?
choices: The first is a user prompt, because it describes the user's bank. The second is a system prompt, because it starts the turn.
Both are system prompts, because the app sends both of them to the model.
The first is a system prompt that sets lasting role and rules. The second is a user prompt for this one turn.
The first is grounding data and the second is a few-shot example.
questions.why: A system prompt is the instruction the app sends to set the model's role, rules and format, and the end user normally does not see it, while a user prompt is the person's message for a single turn.

questions.prompt: Woodgrove Travel's chat assistant, built on a model deployed in Microsoft Foundry, sometimes quotes hotel prices that do not exist. The system prompt already gives a role and limits replies to Woodgrove bookings. Which prompt technique best helps the model answer from Woodgrove's real prices instead of inventing them?
choices: Change the output format to a bulleted list.
Ask customers to type 'use real prices' at the end of every question.
Include the current price list for the relevant hotels in the prompt, so the model answers from that data.
Make the role description longer and friendlier.
questions.why: Supplying relevant facts in the prompt is called grounding, and it lets the model answer from your data rather than filling the gap with a made-up guess.

questions.prompt: Litware Games' help bot has a clear system prompt: 'Answer only questions about Litware games.' In testing, one user keeps pushing, step by step, until the bot writes an unrelated poem. What is the most accurate conclusion?
choices: The team should move the rule into the user prompt, because user prompts override system prompts permanently.
Nothing can be done, because a model ignores any instruction it is given before the user speaks.
A system prompt guides the model but cannot guarantee obedience, so the team should keep refining the prompt and testing it with realistic and tricky questions.
The system prompt must have been ignored completely, because a working system prompt always forces the model to obey.
questions.why: A system prompt shapes behaviour but does not guarantee it, and a determined user can sometimes talk the model off course, which is why iterating on the prompt and testing it is part of the job.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why the chatbot needs a system prompt at all when users can just type what they want. Explain the difference between system and user prompts, what makes a prompt effective, and one limit of relying on prompts.
lessons.modelAnswer: The system prompt is the app's standing briefing, and it is sent with every conversation. It sets the assistant's role, its scope, its tone, the output format, and what to do when it doesn't know. The user prompt is just the person's request for that turn. Without a system prompt, the model has no idea it works for us, so it gives generic, inconsistent answers. Users shouldn't have to repeat our rules every time. An effective prompt is specific. It names the role, states the constraints and the length, shows the format or a few examples, and grounds the model with our real facts, such as the 30-day return policy, so it doesn't invent them. The limit is that a prompt steers the model but doesn't enforce anything. The model can still drift, make things up, or be talked out of its instructions. So we test the prompt with realistic questions, keep refining it, and don't treat it as a security boundary.
rubricPoints: The system prompt sets lasting role, rules and format for every conversation, while the user prompt is the per-turn request.
Effective prompts are specific about role, scope, length and output format.
Few-shot examples and grounding with real facts improve accuracy and consistency.
Vague prompts produce generic, inconsistent or invented answers.
Prompts guide but do not guarantee behaviour, so they need testing and iteration.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine exercises prompt writing, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which prompt change fixes a given model behaviour builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Deploying a model means taking a ready-made AI model from a shared shelf and setting up your own private, running copy of it that you can actually send questions to. Think of a library catalogue: browsing the catalogue shows you every book, but you cannot read one until you check it out under your name. In Microsoft Foundry, the web-based workspace for building AI apps, you pick a model from its catalogue, deploy it under a name you choose, and then chat with it in a test area called the playground to see how it behaves before writing any app.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a model appears in a catalogue of available AI models, do you think you can send it a question straight away, or must you do something first? What might that step be?
lessons.teach:
Deploying a model in Microsoft Foundry means creating a named, running endpoint for one model inside your project so that it can receive requests. A project is your working space in Foundry that holds your resources and settings. The model catalog is the list of models you can choose from, such as chat models from various providers. A deployment is your own instance of a chosen model; it has a deployment name you pick, and an endpoint, which is the web address requests are sent to. Each deployment has a quota, a usage limit often measured in tokens per minute, where a token is a small chunk of text roughly the size of part of a word.

Why a separate step? The catalogue only describes models. Deploying reserves capacity, applies your quota, and links usage to your billing, so nothing runs or costs money until you choose it.

Worked example: you open your project, browse the catalog, and select a chat model. You choose Deploy, name it support-chat, and accept a modest token-per-minute limit. Foundry creates the endpoint. You open the chat playground, an in-portal test screen, pick support-chat, and type a system message, which is a standing instruction such as "You answer billing questions politely." You then type a user message, "Why was I charged twice?", and read the reply. You adjust parameters, which are settings that shape output, like temperature (higher means more varied wording) and maximum response length, and try again to compare.

A common mistake is confusing the model name with the deployment name. Apps and the playground address your deployment, so a client that asks for the model name instead of support-chat fails with a not-found error. Another consequence in a running system: if real traffic exceeds the quota you set, requests are throttled, meaning rejected until the limit resets, so the quota chosen at deployment time directly limits how many users you can serve.

questions.prompt: A city library wants a chat assistant that helps visitors find books. A staff member works through these steps in Microsoft Foundry. Step 1: She opens the library's project, the working space that holds its resources and settings. Step 2: She browses the model catalog, the list of available models, and selects a chat model. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: She opens the chat playground, the in-portal test screen, and picks library-helper from the list. Step 5: She enters the system message "You help visitors find books by topic" and the user message "Where are the cookbooks?", then reads the reply. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Set the temperature to a high value so the model is ready to accept requests
Choose Deploy, name the deployment library-helper, and accept a token-per-minute limit
Nothing is needed; selecting a model in the catalog makes it appear in the playground
Type the system message into the catalog page so the model starts running
questions.why: The catalog only describes models, so a deployment named library-helper, with its endpoint and quota, must be created before the playground can send requests to it.

questions.prompt: A school's IT team finds a chat model they like in the Microsoft Foundry model catalog. Before any app can send requests to that model, what must exist?
choices: Only the catalog listing, because catalog models accept requests directly
A system message saved in the chat playground for that model
A deployment of the model in their project, with a chosen name and an endpoint
A higher temperature setting saved on the catalog entry for that model
questions.why: Deploying creates the named, running endpoint that receives requests, reserves capacity, and applies quota; a catalog listing alone runs nothing.

questions.prompt: A logistics company deployed a chat model in Foundry under the deployment name route-helper. Their client app sends requests that ask for the underlying model's name and gets a not-found error. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Raise the deployment's tokens-per-minute quota
Lower the temperature so replies are less varied
Add a system message describing the routing task
Change the client so it addresses route-helper
questions.why: Apps address the deployment name, not the model name, so asking for the model name returns not-found until the client uses route-helper.

questions.prompt: An event-ticket website deployed a chat model in Foundry with a quota of 20,000 tokens per minute (a token is a small chunk of text). On a busy sale day, real traffic needs far more tokens per minute than that. What happens to the extra requests?
choices: They are throttled, meaning rejected until the limit resets
The deployment is deleted and must be created again
The model automatically shortens every reply to fit the limit
They are served normally but billed at a higher rate
questions.why: Traffic beyond the quota set at deployment time is throttled, which caps how many users the deployment can serve.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what deploying a model in Foundry actually does and why the playground is useful, and name one limit or tradeoff they must keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: Picking a model in the Foundry catalog doesn't make it usable; you have to deploy it. Deploying creates our own named instance with an endpoint, and it ties the model to our project's quota and billing. The deployment name is what everything calls, so our app must use that name, not the underlying model's name, or it gets a not-found error. Once deployed, the chat playground lets us test it without code: we set a system message for its standing instructions, send user messages, and tweak parameters like temperature and maximum response length to see how answers change. The tradeoff is capacity and cost. The tokens-per-minute quota we set caps throughput, so if real traffic goes over it, requests get throttled. A bigger quota serves more users but can consume more of our allowance and cost more.
rubricPoints: States that the catalogue lists models but a deployment is needed before the model can be called.
Explains that a deployment has its own name and endpoint, and clients use the deployment name.
Describes the playground as a no-code place to test prompts, including a system message and user message.
Mentions adjusting parameters such as temperature or maximum response length.
Names a limit such as the tokens-per-minute quota causing throttling, or the cost of capacity.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly portal steps and terms (catalog, deployment, playground, quota) with no matching OpsForge mission or planned engine, so careful reading is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A lightweight chat client is a small program, often a few dozen lines, that lets a person type a message, sends it to an AI model you have already deployed in Microsoft Foundry, and prints the reply. The Foundry SDK (software development kit, a ready-made code library) handles connecting and signing in for you. Think of it like a phone: the model is the expert on the other end, the SDK is the phone line, and your app just dials, speaks, and listens. One surprise is that the model forgets each call, so your app must remember the conversation and repeat it each time.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you send a model the message 'What is my name?' right after an earlier call where you said 'My name is Ana', but you only send the new message, do you think the model will know your name? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A lightweight chat client is a minimal application that sends user messages to a deployed generative model and shows the replies. In Microsoft Foundry, a project is the workspace that holds your resources, and it has a project endpoint, the web address your code connects to. A deployment is a named, running copy of a model inside that project; your code refers to the deployment name, not just the model family name.

The Foundry SDK is a code library that wraps these calls. The usual flow is: create a credential (proof of identity, typically a Microsoft Entra ID sign-in rather than a pasted key), create a project client from the endpoint and credential, ask the project client for a chat-capable client (an OpenAI-compatible client, meaning it speaks the same request format as OpenAI's API), then send a request containing the deployment name and a list of messages.

Each message has a role. The system role sets standing instructions, the user role carries what the person typed, and the assistant role holds the model's earlier replies. This works because the model endpoint is stateless: it remembers nothing between calls, so the full history in the list is its only context.

Worked example. Step 1: the list starts with a system message, 'You are a helpful travel assistant.' Step 2: the user types 'Suggest a city in Portugal'; the app appends it as a user message and sends the list. Step 3: the reply 'Porto' comes back; the app prints it and appends it as an assistant message. Step 4: the user types 'What food is it known for?'; the app appends this and sends all four messages, so the model knows 'it' means Porto.

A common mistake is sending only the newest user message each turn. The app still runs, but answers lose context and follow-up questions fail. The opposite tradeoff matters in a running system: history grows every turn, so requests get larger, slower and costlier, and eventually exceed the model's context limit, which is why real clients trim or summarize old turns.

questions.prompt: A plant nursery called Greenleaf builds a small chat client with the Foundry SDK. Its deployment is named 'garden-helper'. The app's message list begins with one system message: 'You answer questions about houseplants.' Turn 1: the customer types 'Which plant suits a dark hallway?' The app appends this as a user message, sends the list, gets back 'A snake plant', prints it, and appends it as an assistant message. Turn 2: the customer types 'How often should I water it?' and the app appends this as a user message. MISSING STEP: what should the app send to the 'garden-helper' deployment now?
choices: The system message plus the new user message, leaving out the earlier exchange to save space
Only the new user message 'How often should I water it?', because the model already saw the earlier turns
The first and second user messages only, because assistant replies came from the model and need not be resent
All four messages: the system message, the first user message, the assistant reply 'A snake plant', and the new user message
questions.why: The model endpoint is stateless, so only by receiving the whole history, including the assistant's 'A snake plant', can it work out that 'it' means the snake plant.

questions.prompt: At Northwind Logistics, a project in Microsoft Foundry holds a model from the gpt-4o family, deployed under the name 'dispatch-chat-02'. When the chat client sends a request, which value should it give to identify the model?
choices: The project endpoint web address
The name of the Microsoft Entra ID account used to sign in
'dispatch-chat-02', the deployment name
'gpt-4o', the model family name
questions.why: A deployment is the named, running copy of the model in the project, and the request refers to that deployment name rather than the model family name.

questions.prompt: A city library's chat client answers 'Do you have books on beekeeping?' correctly. But when the patron then asks 'Can I reserve one of them?', the reply makes no sense, as if the earlier question never happened. The app shows no errors. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The deployment name was misspelled in the second request
The system message was written in the user role instead
Each turn sends only the newest user message instead of the full history
The credential expired between the two turns
questions.why: Because the endpoint remembers nothing between calls, sending only the newest message leaves the model unable to tell what 'them' refers to, even though the app still runs.

questions.prompt: A bank's internal help chat client resends the full conversation every turn. In very long sessions, around turn 150, staff notice replies getting slower and costing more, and eventually requests start failing. What explains this, and what do real clients usually do about it?
choices: The model gradually forgets earlier turns on its own, so the client should send only the newest message
The project endpoint stores every session and runs out of room, so the client should create a new project each day
The growing history makes each request bigger until it passes the model's context limit, so clients trim or summarize older turns
Assistant messages slow the model down, so the client should stop sending the system message
questions.why: The history grows every turn, so each request gets larger, slower and costlier until it exceeds the context limit, and trimming or summarizing old turns keeps requests within that limit.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a lightweight chat client built with the Foundry SDK keeps a conversation going, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The client signs in with a credential, usually Entra ID, connects to the Foundry project endpoint with a project client, and gets an OpenAI-compatible chat client from it. Each request names the model deployment and sends a list of messages with roles: a system message for standing instructions, user messages for what the person typed, and assistant messages for earlier replies. The model endpoint is stateless, so it only knows what is in that list. That means our app must append every user message and every reply and resend the whole history each turn, otherwise follow-ups like 'what about it?' lose their meaning. The tradeoff is that history keeps growing: each call gets bigger, slower and more expensive, and eventually hits the model's context limit, so we need to trim or summarize older turns.
rubricPoints: The client authenticates with a credential and connects through the project endpoint using the SDK's project client.
Requests target a named model deployment, not just a model family.
Messages carry roles: system for instructions, user for input, assistant for prior replies.
The model is stateless, so the app must store and resend the conversation history.
Growing history increases cost and latency and can exceed the context limit, so it must be trimmed or summarized.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine calls a deployed model, and the core understanding to check is the client flow and why the app must carry conversation history, which explaining back tests well.

lessons.plain: An AI agent is a chat assistant built around a language model that has been given a job description, some reference material and some tools it may use. Creating a single agent in the Foundry portal means filling in a form in Microsoft's web workspace: choose a model you have already deployed, write the agent's standing instructions, and attach any tools. Testing means chatting with it in a built-in practice window before anyone else sees it. Think of hiring a new receptionist: you hand them a rulebook and a binder of house policies, then run a few pretend phone calls to check they answer correctly.
lessons.guessPrompt: You build a hotel help agent and upload a PDF of the hotel's pet policy, but you never switch on a tool that lets the agent search files. A tester asks whether dogs are allowed. What do you expect the agent to do, and why?
lessons.teach:
In Microsoft Foundry, an agent is a configured assistant made of four parts. The model is the deployed language model that generates text; you must deploy one first because the agent only points at an existing deployment. The instructions are a standing system message describing role, tone and limits, applied to every conversation. Tools are extra abilities the agent may decide to call, such as file search (looks up passages in documents you upload, a form of grounding, which means basing answers on supplied sources), code interpreter (runs code to calculate or chart), or web search. A thread is one conversation's stored message history, so the agent remembers earlier turns within it.

This works because the agent service wraps the model: on each message it sends the instructions plus the thread history, lets the model choose tools, feeds tool results back, and returns the final reply.

Worked example. Step 1: open your Foundry project and go to the Agents area. Step 2: create a new agent, name it Hotel Helper, and select your deployed chat model. Step 3: write instructions such as: answer guest questions using only the hotel policy files; if unsure, say so and suggest the front desk. Step 4: add the file search tool and upload the policy PDF. Step 5: open the playground, the built-in test chat. Ask an in-scope question (are dogs allowed?) and check the answer matches the PDF. Ask a follow-up (what about cats?) to confirm the thread keeps context. Ask something out of scope (best pizza nearby?) to confirm it declines politely. Start a new thread to confirm memory resets.

A common mistake is uploading documents or writing facts in the instructions but never enabling the tool that reads those documents, or only testing happy-path questions. The agent then answers from the model's general knowledge. In a live system that means confident but wrong answers reaching real users, so testing out-of-scope and tricky questions in the playground is part of creating the agent, not an optional extra.

questions.prompt: A bike-repair shop wants a Foundry agent called Spoke Support that answers customer questions using only its 12-page warranty guide. Here is the plan, with one step missing. Step 1: [missing]. Step 2: In the project's Agents area, create the agent named Spoke Support and point it at that chat-model deployment. Step 3: Write instructions saying it should answer warranty questions only from the guide, and if unsure, tell the customer to phone the workshop. Step 4: Add the file search tool and upload the warranty guide. Step 5: In the playground, ask an in-scope question about frame cracks, a follow-up about forks, and an unrelated question about cycling routes. Then start a new thread. What is Step 1?
choices: Start a new thread in the playground so the agent has an empty message history.
Paste the full warranty guide into the instructions so the agent has the facts.
Deploy a chat language model in the Foundry project.
Add the code interpreter tool so the agent can open and read the PDF.
questions.why: An agent only points at an existing model deployment, so a chat model must be deployed before the agent can select it in Step 2.

questions.prompt: A city council tests its Bin Day agent in the Foundry playground. A resident asks, "When is green waste collected?" and then, "And glass?" The agent understands that the second question is also about collection days. Which part of the agent makes this possible?
choices: The file search tool, which looks up passages in uploaded documents
The model deployment, which keeps its own memory across all users
The thread, which stores this conversation's message history
The instructions, which are a standing system message applied to every conversation
questions.why: A thread is one conversation's stored message history, so the agent remembers earlier turns within that conversation.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm builds a Foundry agent for staff. Given a list of 40 invoice amounts, it must add them up and produce a bar chart of totals by month. Which tool should the firm enable for this?
choices: File search, because the invoices are a kind of document
No tool, because writing the steps into the instructions is enough
Code interpreter, because it runs code to calculate and chart
Web search, because it can look up current exchange rates
questions.why: Code interpreter lets the agent run code, which is the tool for doing calculations and drawing charts.

questions.prompt: A gym writes instructions for its Member Desk agent that say, "Answer only from the uploaded membership rules," and uploads a 30-page rules document to the project. However, the file search tool is never added to the agent. In the playground, the agent confidently says the cancellation fee is 20 dollars, but the rules say 35. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The playground cannot test agents that have documents uploaded.
The instructions must be rewritten as a tool before they take effect.
Without the file search tool, the agent answers from the model's general knowledge.
The thread was too short for the agent to remember the rules.
questions.why: Documents are only read through the file search tool. Without it, the agent falls back on the model's general knowledge and can give confident but wrong answers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you configure when you create a single agent in the Foundry portal and how you would test it before release, naming one limit of playground testing.
lessons.modelAnswer: An agent in Foundry is a deployed model plus a set of standing instructions plus optional tools. I first need a model deployment, then in the Agents area I create the agent, pick that deployment, and write instructions that set its role, tone and boundaries. If it must answer from our documents, I add the file search tool and upload them, so its answers are grounded in our content rather than general knowledge. Then I test in the playground: in-scope questions checked against the source, follow-ups to see the thread keeps context, out-of-scope questions to see it declines, and a fresh thread to confirm memory resets. The limit is that a handful of manual playground chats is a small sample; it cannot prove the agent behaves well across every phrasing real users will try, so I treat it as a first check, not a guarantee.
rubricPoints: Defines an agent as a deployed model plus instructions plus optional tools.
Notes a model must be deployed before the agent can use it.
Explains that attached documents need a tool such as file search to be used for grounding.
Describes testing in the playground with in-scope, follow-up and out-of-scope questions.
Mentions that a thread holds conversation history and a new thread starts fresh.
Names a limit, such as manual playground tests being a small sample of real usage.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine recreates the Foundry agent setup, and the objective is mainly portal steps and their purpose, so careful reading with the worked example fits best.

lessons.plain: An agent is an AI helper you set up once in Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft's platform for building AI apps. You give it a model, written instructions, and optional tools such as file search. A lightweight client application is a small program, such as a console script or simple web page, that lets people talk to that agent. The client does not contain the AI. Think of a phone: the phone is the client and the expert on the other end is the agent. The phone just dials the right number, passes your words along, and plays back the answer. It also keeps the call open, so the expert remembers what you already said.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a small program sends a user's second question to an agent, how would the agent know what the first question was?
lessons.teach:
A lightweight client for an agent is a small program that connects to an agent already defined in a Microsoft Foundry project. It sends user messages to the agent and shows the agent's replies. The agent's model, instructions and tools live in the Foundry service, not in the client.

The client uses a few named pieces. The project endpoint is the web address of your Foundry project. Authentication proves who the client is. The usual way is Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's identity service. The Foundry SDK, a code library Microsoft publishes for Python and other languages, can pick up your signed-in identity, so no secret key sits in the code. The agent reference is the agent's name or ID. A conversation, also called a thread, is a stored history of messages kept by the service. A run, also called a response, is one request asking the agent to process the conversation and reply.

This design works because the service holds the conversation state. The client only has to remember one conversation ID.

Here is a worked example: a helpdesk console app.
Step 1: The app connects to the project endpoint with the user's Entra identity.
Step 2: It looks up the agent named helpdesk-agent.
Step 3: It creates a conversation and stores that conversation's ID.
Step 4: The user types "My laptop won't connect to VPN." The app adds this message to the conversation and starts a run.
Step 5: The agent reads its instructions and may call a tool. The app gets the reply and prints it.
Step 6: The user types "I tried that already." The app adds this to the same conversation. Because the agent sees the earlier messages, it understands what "that" refers to.
Step 7: When the session ends, the app can delete the conversation.

A common mistake is creating a new conversation for every message. The agent then loses context and gives answers that make no sense as follow-ups. A second mistake is creating a brand-new agent each time the app starts. That leaves duplicate agents in the project. Another mistake is pasting secret keys into the source code, where they can leak.

questions.prompt:
A city council builds a small kiosk app so residents can ask questions about building permits. An agent named permit-guide already exists in the council's Foundry project, with its model, instructions and a permit-lookup tool. Here is how the kiosk app works each morning when it starts, with one step missing.
Step 1: The app connects to the council's project endpoint using the kiosk's Microsoft Entra ID identity, with no secret key in the code.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: When a resident walks up, the app creates a conversation and keeps its ID.
Step 4: The resident types "Do I need a permit for a 3-metre fence?" The app adds this message to that conversation and starts a run, then shows the reply.
Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Look up the existing agent permit-guide by its name or ID to get a reference to it.
Create a separate conversation for each message the resident is expected to send that day.
Load the agent's instructions into the kiosk app so they can be sent with every message.
Create a brand-new agent called permit-guide with the model, instructions and tool settings.
questions.why: The agent is already defined in the Foundry project, so the client only needs a reference to it by name or ID; creating a new agent at each start would leave duplicate agents in the project.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain writes a lightweight client for its order-help agent in Foundry. A customer will send several messages in one session. Between those messages, what is the main thing the client app itself needs to keep track of?
choices: The ID of the one conversation (thread) the service is storing for this session
A copy of the agent's model and instructions, so replies stay consistent
The full text of every earlier message, so it can resend the whole history each time
A new run ID for every message, used to open a fresh conversation each time
questions.why: The Foundry service stores the conversation history, so the client only has to remember the single conversation ID.

questions.prompt: A travel agency's client app talks to a trip-planning agent. Testers report that when they type "Make it two nights cheaper" after asking about a hotel in Lisbon, the agent replies as if it has no idea what they mean. The code shows the app creates a new conversation every time the user sends a message. What is the cause?
choices: The app is authenticating with Microsoft Entra ID instead of a secret key
Each new conversation starts empty, so the agent cannot see the earlier messages and loses context
The agent's tools are disabled whenever a new run starts in an existing conversation
The project endpoint is wrong, so the agent receives only part of each message
questions.why: A conversation holds the message history, so starting a new one for each message removes the context the agent needs to understand follow-ups.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling team's client app for its appointment agent currently has a secret key pasted into the source code to connect to the Foundry project. What is the recommended way to authenticate instead?
choices: Move the secret key into a comment so it is not run as code
Send the key as the first message in every conversation
Use Microsoft Entra ID, letting the Foundry SDK pick up the signed-in identity so no key sits in the code
Create a new agent at each start so the key is refreshed automatically
questions.why: Entra ID authentication through the SDK uses the signed-in identity, so there is no secret key in the source code that could leak.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a small client app talks to an agent built in Foundry, and name one limit or tradeoff of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The agent is built in the Foundry project, with its model, instructions and tools, and it lives in the service. Our client is just a thin program that connects to it. It uses the Foundry SDK to connect to the project endpoint and signs in with Entra ID, so we don't hard-code keys. It finds the agent by name or ID, creates a conversation, adds each user message to it, and starts a run to get the reply. We reuse the same conversation ID so the agent keeps context across turns. One tradeoff is that the client depends completely on the service. If the network or the service is slow, the user waits. Long conversations also grow, which costs more tokens, so we should end or delete them when a session is over.
rubricPoints: The agent's model, instructions and tools live in Foundry, not in the client.
The client connects with the project endpoint and Entra ID authentication through the SDK.
The client references an existing agent instead of recreating it.
The client sends messages to a conversation (thread) and starts a run to get a reply.
Reusing the same conversation keeps context across turns.
The answer names a limit, such as service dependency, latency, or conversation growth and cost.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises Foundry agents, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which pieces a client needs, and why conversations are reused, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Text analysis means having software read written words and report what is in them: which language the text is in, whether its tone is positive or negative, which key topics it mentions, and which named things appear, such as people, places, dates or personal details. Think of it as a tireless assistant who reads every customer review and puts a sticky note on each one saying 'English, unhappy, about late delivery, mentions a city.' A lightweight application is a small program that sends text to a hosted language service and acts on the labels it gets back.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a program read the review 'The delivery was late, but the driver was very polite,' what overall mood label do you think it should give, and why might one label not tell the whole story?
lessons.teach:
Text analysis is a set of ready-made language features that turn free text into structured labels. In Microsoft Foundry these come from Azure Language in Foundry Tools, a managed natural-language service: you send text over the internet and get back results without training a model yourself. Language detection names the language. Sentiment analysis scores tone as positive, neutral, negative or mixed, overall and per sentence. Key phrase extraction pulls out the main talking points. Named entity recognition (NER) finds and categorizes things such as people, organizations, locations and dates. PII detection finds personally identifiable information, meaning details that identify a person, like phone numbers, and can mask them.

A lightweight client works like this: it holds the resource endpoint (the service's web address) and a credential (an API key or a Microsoft Entra ID identity), sends one or more documents, and receives JSON, a structured text format, with each label plus a confidence score from 0 to 1 showing how sure the model is. It works because these models were pretrained on large amounts of text, so common tasks need no setup.

Worked example: a support app sends 'The delivery was late, but the driver was very polite.' Step 1: language detection returns English. Step 2: sentiment returns mixed overall; sentence one negative, sentence two positive. Step 3: key phrases return 'delivery' and 'driver'. Step 4: the app routes the ticket to the logistics team because the negative sentence concerns delivery.

You could also ask a deployed generative model to do this with a prompt, but the prebuilt features give consistent labels and scores with less prompt work.

A common mistake is reading only the overall label and ignoring sentence-level results and confidence scores. In a running system, that misroutes mixed complaints or acts on low-confidence guesses, so real issues get ignored. Another mistake is hardcoding the key in source code, where it can leak.

questions.prompt: A city library's feedback app uses the text analysis features in Azure Language in Foundry Tools, a managed natural-language service, to sort visitor comments. A visitor writes: 'The new reading room is beautiful. The Wi-Fi keeps dropping every few minutes.' Step 1: language detection returns English. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: key phrase extraction returns 'reading room' and 'Wi-Fi'. Step 4: the app sends the comment to the IT team, because the negative sentence is about the Wi-Fi. Which result belongs in Step 2?
choices: Sentiment analysis returns positive overall, so no sentence-level results are produced.
Sentiment analysis returns mixed overall, with the first sentence positive and the second sentence negative.
PII detection masks 'Wi-Fi' because it identifies a person.
Named entity recognition returns 'reading room' as a location and 'Wi-Fi' as an organization.
questions.why: Step 4 routes the comment based on which sentence is negative, so Step 2 must be sentiment analysis giving a mixed overall score plus a separate score for each sentence.

questions.prompt: A property firm wants to scan lease agreements and automatically list every company name, city and signing date they mention, each one tagged with its category. Which prebuilt text analysis feature does this?
choices: Named entity recognition (NER)
Language detection
Key phrase extraction
Sentiment analysis
questions.why: Named entity recognition finds things such as organizations, locations and dates in text and puts each one into a category, whereas key phrase extraction only pulls out the main talking points.

questions.prompt: A developer at a small charity writes a short script that sends donor messages to Azure Language in Foundry Tools for sentiment analysis. What must the script hold in order to call the service?
choices: A custom model trained on the charity's past messages, plus the training data used to build it
