A connection string to the charity's database and a local copy of the language model
A GPU, so it can run the sentiment model on the developer's machine
The resource endpoint (the service's web address) and a credential, such as an API key or a Microsoft Entra ID identity
questions.why: A lightweight client only needs the endpoint and a credential. It sends documents over the internet and gets back JSON, with no training or local model needed, because the models are already pretrained.

questions.prompt: An online bank's review sorter automatically closes any feedback ticket whose overall sentiment label is positive. A customer complaint was closed because it came back labeled positive with a confidence score of 0.38. What is the main design flaw?
choices: Confidence scores run from 0 to 100, so 0.38 actually means the model was very sure.
The service needed to be retrained on bank reviews before it could return any sentiment label.
The app should have used language detection instead of sentiment analysis to judge tone.
The app acts on the overall label alone and ignores the low confidence score, so it treats an unsure guess as fact.
questions.why: The confidence score runs from 0 to 1, so 0.38 shows the model was unsure. Acting on a low-confidence label without checking the score, or the sentence-level results, means real complaints get ignored.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a small app would use Foundry's text analysis to triage customer reviews, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: For review triage, I'd use Azure Language in Foundry Tools, which is a managed language service with prebuilt features. Our app keeps the endpoint and a credential, ideally an Entra ID identity or a key stored outside the code, and sends each review as a document. It gets JSON back: the detected language, sentiment overall and per sentence, key phrases, and named entities, plus PII detection if we need to mask personal details. Each result carries a confidence score. We route on those labels, for example negative sentences about delivery go to logistics. The tradeoff is that these are prebuilt, general models: they're quick and consistent but not tailored to our wording, and they can be wrong. So we shouldn't trust only the overall label. Mixed reviews need sentence-level results, and low-confidence results should go to a human instead of being acted on automatically.
rubricPoints: Names the managed language service in Foundry (Azure Language) as the capability used.
Lists relevant features such as sentiment, key phrases, entities, language detection or PII detection.
Describes the client calling an endpoint with a credential and receiving structured JSON.
Mentions confidence scores and sentence-level results rather than one overall label.
States a limit, such as generic models making mistakes or needing human review for low confidence.
Notes keeping credentials out of source code.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises a language service, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which text feature fits a task builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Responding to spoken prompts means a person talks instead of types, and an AI model listens to the recording and answers. Some generative AI models are multimodal, meaning they accept more than one kind of input, such as text, images or audio, in the same request. If you deploy one that understands audio, your app can hand it a voice clip directly, the way you might pass a voicemail to a colleague and ask for a reply, rather than first typing out what was said. The model hears the question, works out the meaning and writes back an answer, and some models can also speak the answer aloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a user records the question "Is it warm enough for a picnic tomorrow?", what two things do you think your app must send to an audio-capable AI model so it can answer?
lessons.teach:
A spoken prompt is a question or instruction delivered as an audio recording. A multimodal model is a generative model that accepts several input types in one request. In Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft's platform for deploying and using AI models, you create a deployment, which is a named, callable instance of a model with its own endpoint (the web address your app sends requests to). To answer speech directly, that deployment must be an audio-capable model, such as a GPT-4o model variant that supports audio input.

It works because the model was trained on audio as well as text, so it can pull meaning straight from the sound without a separate transcription step. The request follows the normal chat format: a list of messages, each with a role (system, user or assistant). The user message can hold several content parts, for example one text part and one audio part.

Worked example: a user records a WAV file asking about a picnic. First, the app reads the file's bytes. Second, it base64-encodes them, turning the binary audio into plain text that can travel inside a request. Third, it builds the messages: a system message that sets behaviour ("You are a friendly weather helper"), then a user message containing a text part ("Answer the question in this recording") and an audio part with the encoded data and its format, wav. Fourth, it sends this to the deployment's endpoint with a key or signed-in identity. Fifth, the model returns a text reply, which the app shows. If the model and request allow it, the app can also ask for spoken output.

A common mistake is sending audio to a text-only deployment, or labelling the format wrongly. The request is rejected or the audio is misread, and the running app fails exactly when users speak. The alternative design is a pipeline: a dedicated speech service converts speech to text, a text model answers, and the speech service converts the answer back to speech. That gives more control, such as custom vocabulary and saved transcripts, at the cost of extra moving parts.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain, Harbourline Hotels, adds a voice concierge to its booking app. A guest records a 9-second MP3 asking whether the rooftop pool is open late. Here is what the app does: (1) It sends requests to a Foundry deployment named concierge-audio, which runs an audio-capable GPT-4o variant. (2) It reads the MP3 file's bytes. (3) It base64-encodes those bytes. (4) It builds a system message: "You are a polite hotel concierge." (5) It builds a user message with a text part, "Reply to the guest's recorded question," and an audio part that holds the encoded data and a format label. (6) It sends the request to the deployment's endpoint with a key. (7) It shows the model's text reply to the guest. The missing step: what value should the format label in step 5 hold?
choices: wav, because WAV is the standard label for spoken prompts
base64, because the audio data was base64-encoded in step 3
text, because base64 turns the audio into plain text
mp3, matching the actual format of the guest's recording
questions.why: The format label must describe the real audio format of the recording, which is MP3; base64 is only how the bytes travel, and a wrong label makes the audio misread or rejected.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Tallis Freight, wants drivers to ask spoken questions about delivery routes and get answers. One engineer proposes sending the audio straight to a deployed GPT-4o audio-capable model. Why can that model answer the spoken question without a separate transcription step?
choices: The base64 encoding converts the speech into readable words before the model sees it
The system message tells the model to transcribe the audio before answering it
It was trained on audio as well as text, so it can take meaning directly from the sound
Foundry automatically runs a speech-to-text service in front of every deployment
questions.why: A multimodal, audio-capable model learned from audio as well as text, so it understands speech directly; base64 only packages bytes and does not transcribe anything.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy group, Meridian Health, is building a phone assistant that answers spoken questions about medicines. It must recognise unusual drug names reliably and keep a written transcript of every call for audit. Which design best fits these needs?
choices: Base64-encode the audio and place it inside the system message of a chat request
Use a pipeline: a speech service converts speech to text, a text model answers, then speech output is generated
Send the audio to a text-only deployment with the format labelled as text
Send the audio directly to an audio-capable multimodal deployment and display its reply
questions.why: A speech-service pipeline gives extra control such as custom vocabulary and saved transcripts, at the cost of more moving parts.

questions.prompt: A city library, Northgate Libraries, launches a help app. Typed questions work well, but every time a visitor submits a voice recording the request fails. The audio part is correctly encoded and labelled. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The app forgot to include a system message in the request
The deployment runs a text-only model that cannot accept audio input
The user message contained both a text part and an audio part
The model returned a text reply instead of spoken output
questions.why: Sending audio to a text-only deployment causes rejection, so the app fails exactly when users speak; mixing text and audio parts in one user message is normal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how our app can answer a user's spoken question using a deployed multimodal model in Foundry, and name one limit or tradeoff compared with using a separate speech-to-text service first.
lessons.modelAnswer: We deploy an audio-capable multimodal model in Foundry, which gives us an endpoint. When a user speaks, the app reads the recording, base64-encodes it so it fits in the request, and sends a chat request: a system message setting the assistant's behaviour, then a user message with a short text instruction plus an audio part carrying the encoded clip and its format, like wav. The model understands the audio directly and replies with text, and optionally speech if we ask for it. The main tradeoff is control. It is one simple call, but we get no separate transcript to log or check, and fewer options such as custom vocabulary for product names. A pipeline using a dedicated speech service gives us those, but it adds more services and more steps that can fail. We also have to make sure the deployment actually supports audio.
rubricPoints: States that the deployment must be a multimodal model that accepts audio input.
Describes encoding the recording and sending it as an audio content part with its format.
Mentions the chat message structure with a system message and a user message.
Notes the model replies with text and can optionally produce speech.
Names a tradeoff versus a speech-to-text pipeline, such as less control, no transcript or no custom vocabulary.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine sends audio to a model, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about when to use a direct multimodal call versus a speech-service pipeline builds the most useful judgement.

lessons.plain: Azure Speech is a ready-made cloud service, offered inside Microsoft Foundry's set of tools, that turns spoken audio into written text and written text into natural-sounding speech. You don't train anything; you send audio or text to the service and get the converted result back. Think of it as a hired interpreter between voice and writing: you hand over a recording and get a transcript, or hand over a script and get a voice reading it. A 'lightweight application' here just means a small program that connects to this service, sends it the input, and uses the result, such as a voice-controlled note taker or an app that reads messages aloud.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted a small app to read a written news article out loud, which direction of conversion would it need (speech to text, or text to speech), and what choice about how it sounds would you probably want to make?
lessons.teach:
Azure Speech in Foundry Tools is a prebuilt, managed speech service. Prebuilt means Microsoft has already trained the models; managed means you call it over the network without running servers. It offers two core capabilities. Speech to text (speech recognition) converts audio into a transcript. Text to speech (speech synthesis) converts text into spoken audio using a chosen voice, which is a named synthetic speaker with a language and style.

A lightweight client calls it through the Speech SDK, a code library that handles the audio streaming for you. The client first builds a configuration object holding three things: the endpoint (the web address of your Speech resource) or its region, a credential such as a key or a signed-in identity, and settings like the recognition language (for example en-US) or the voice name. From that configuration it creates either a recognizer, which listens to a microphone or audio file and returns text, or a synthesizer, which takes text and plays or saves audio.

Worked example: a hands-free note app. Step 1, the app loads the endpoint and key from settings. Step 2, it sets recognition language to en-US and creates a recognizer on the default microphone. Step 3, the user says 'Buy milk tomorrow'; the service returns the text 'Buy milk tomorrow.' and a result status of recognized. Step 4, the app saves the note, then creates a synthesizer with an English voice and speaks 'Note saved.'

A common mistake is mismatching settings: using a key from one resource with another resource's endpoint or region, or leaving the recognition language wrong for the speaker. The running system then fails with authentication errors or returns poor, garbled transcripts, so always check the result status rather than assuming success. Note that this service converts between voice and text; answering a spoken question with reasoning is a separate job for a deployed multimodal model.

questions.prompt: A city museum builds a small audio-guide app that reads exhibit descriptions aloud in French. Step 1: the app loads its Speech resource endpoint and key from settings. Step 2: it sets the voice name to a French voice in the configuration object. Step 3: ??? Step 4: it passes the 120-word description of exhibit 14 as text and saves the returned spoken audio to a file for visitors to play. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Create a recognizer on the default microphone from the configuration
Create a synthesizer from the configuration
Set the recognition language to fr-FR and wait for a transcript
Deploy a multimodal model to reason about the exhibit text
questions.why: Turning text into spoken audio is text to speech, so the client must create a synthesizer from the configuration before it can pass in the description text.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic has 300 recorded audio files of vets dictating case notes and wants each one turned into written text using Azure Speech in Foundry Tools. After building the configuration object, what should its lightweight client create?
choices: A new voice with a language and style for each vet
A server that hosts its own trained speech model
A recognizer that reads each audio file and returns text
A synthesizer that takes each file and plays it back
questions.why: Converting audio into a transcript is speech to text, and a recognizer listens to a microphone or audio file and returns text, with no servers to run because the service is managed.

questions.prompt: A delivery company's driver app fails every speech request with authentication errors. The configuration uses the endpoint of the company's Speech resource in one region but a key copied from a different Speech resource the team created for testing. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The key and the endpoint belong to different resources, so they do not match
The app created a synthesizer instead of a recognizer
The prebuilt models must first be retrained on the drivers' voices
The recognition language is set wrong, which always causes authentication errors
questions.why: Using a key from one resource with another resource's endpoint or region is a settings mismatch that leads to authentication errors, whereas a wrong language tends to produce garbled transcripts rather than failed sign-in.

questions.prompt: A bank wants a kiosk where a customer asks aloud, 'Which of my savings accounts earns more interest?', and receives a thought-out spoken answer. Which statement about Azure Speech in Foundry Tools fits this goal?
choices: Speech alone can do it, as long as the recognition language matches the customer
Speech can convert the voice and text, but the reasoning needs a deployed multimodal model
Speech alone can do it, because a synthesizer reasons about the question before speaking
It needs no other piece, because the recognizer returns answers instead of transcripts
questions.why: Azure Speech only converts between voice and text, so producing a reasoned answer to a spoken question is a separate job for a deployed multimodal model.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a small app would use Azure Speech in Foundry Tools to listen to a user and talk back, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on this service.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Speech is a prebuilt, managed service, so we don't train models; we just call it. Our app uses the Speech SDK and first builds a configuration with our resource's endpoint or region, a credential, and settings like the recognition language and the voice we want. For listening, we create a recognizer pointed at the microphone; it streams audio to the service and gets back a transcript plus a status we should check. For talking back, we create a synthesizer, pass it text, and it plays audio in the chosen voice. The tradeoff is that the service only converts between speech and text; it doesn't understand or answer the question, so for real replies we'd add a generative model. It also depends on correct settings and the network: a wrong language gives bad transcripts, and a key and endpoint mismatch fails authentication.
rubricPoints: Identifies Azure Speech as a prebuilt managed service for speech to text and text to speech.
Says the client builds a configuration with endpoint or region, credential, and language or voice.
Distinguishes a recognizer (audio to text) from a synthesizer (text to audio).
Mentions checking the result status instead of assuming success.
Names a limit, such as conversion only with no reasoning, or dependence on correct language, credentials and network.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises speech services, and the exam skill is matching a voice scenario to the right Speech capability and client setup, which exam-style situations train best.

lessons.plain: A multimodal model is an AI model that can take in more than one kind of input, such as text and pictures, in the same request. Interpreting visual input means you hand the model an image together with a question, and it answers in words about what it sees: describing a scene, reading a sign, comparing two photos, or spotting a problem. Think of it like texting a knowledgeable friend a photo and asking, what is this? In Microsoft Foundry, you first deploy such a model, then send it messages that carry both your words and your image.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you send a chat model a photo of a car dashboard plus the question 'Which warning lights are on?', what two things must be true about the model and the message for it to answer from the picture rather than guess?
lessons.teach:
A multimodal model accepts several input types, here text and images, and produces a text answer. Microsoft Foundry is Microsoft's platform for choosing, deploying and calling AI models. A deployment is a named, running copy of a model that your app calls by name. Only a deployment of a vision-capable model can read images; a text-only model will reject or ignore them.

It works because the model was trained on huge numbers of paired images and text, so it learned to link visual patterns to words. In a request, the user message is split into content parts: a text part holding your question and an image part holding the picture. The image is supplied either as a web address the service can reach, or as the file's bytes encoded as text (base64) inside a data URL. A detail setting can trade accuracy for cost, since images are converted into tokens, the units you pay for and that count against the model's size limit.

Worked example. A fleet app wants to know which dashboard warnings are lit. Step 1: deploy a vision-capable model in Foundry and test it in the portal's chat playground by attaching a photo. Step 2: in the client, build one user message with a text part, 'List any warning lights that are on,' and an image part with the photo encoded as base64. Step 3: send it to the deployment. Step 4: the model replies, for example, 'The engine and low-tyre-pressure lights are on.' Step 5: the app shows that text to the driver.

A common mistake is putting a local file path like C:\photos\dash.jpg in the request; the cloud service cannot open your disk, so you must send a reachable URL or the encoded bytes.

In a running system, remember the model can misread small text or invent details. Large images also raise cost and latency, so resize them and have a person verify answers that matter.

questions.prompt: A garden-centre chain is building a phone app that tells staff which plant labels on a shelf are missing prices. The team has deployed a vision-capable model in Microsoft Foundry under the deployment name 'shelf-checker'. A staff member takes a photo, and the phone saves it at /storage/DCIM/aisle7.jpg. The developer reasons through the request like this. First, the request needs one user message split into content parts. Second, the text part holds the question: 'Which plant labels in this photo show no price?' Third, the image part must hold the photo itself, but the service runs in the cloud, so [MISSING STEP]. Fourth, the message is sent to the 'shelf-checker' deployment, and the model replies with text such as 'The two labels on the bottom row show no price.' Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: so the photo should be described in words inside the text part, because content parts can only hold text
so the app reads the file's bytes, encodes them as base64 and places them in a data URL in the image part
so the photo should be sent in a separate second request, after the text question has been answered
so the image part should contain the path /storage/DCIM/aisle7.jpg, because the service opens the file from that location
questions.why: A cloud service cannot open a file path on the user's device, so the image must be sent as a URL the service can reach or as base64-encoded bytes inside a data URL, alongside the text part in the same message.

questions.prompt: A recycling company deploys a model in Microsoft Foundry and sends it a message with a text part, 'What type of plastic is shown?', and an image part containing a photo of a bottle. The reply ignores the photo and only talks about plastics in general. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The deployment is of a text-only model, which rejects or ignores images
The photo was sent as base64-encoded bytes inside a data URL
The text part and the image part were placed in the same user message
The question should have been placed inside the image part instead
questions.why: Only a deployment of a vision-capable (multimodal) model can read images; a text-only model will reject or ignore them, while sending text and image parts together and using base64 are both correct practice.

questions.prompt: A museum app sends very large, high-resolution photos of paintings to a vision-capable model deployment, and the team notices high bills and slow answers. Based on how images are processed, which change best addresses both problems?
choices: Resize the images and use the detail setting to trade some accuracy for lower cost
Switch the deployment to a text-only model so images are processed more cheaply
Send the photos as local file paths so the service does not have to download them
Move the question text into the image part so the request has fewer content parts
questions.why: Images are converted into tokens, the units you pay for and that count against the model's size limit, so smaller images and a lower detail setting reduce cost and latency.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy wants a vision-capable model to read the dosage printed in small type on medicine box photos and show it to customers. What is the most responsible way to run this in production?
choices: Trust the replies fully, since a vision-capable model reads printed text without errors
Use a text-only model deployment, because it is more accurate for reading printed numbers
Send the photos at the largest size possible so the model can never misread them
Have a person verify the dosage answers, because the model can misread small text or invent details
questions.why: A multimodal model can misread small text or invent details, so answers that matter, such as a medicine dosage, should be checked by a person.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how your app gets a deployed Foundry model to answer a question about a photo, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: First we need a deployment of a multimodal, vision-capable model in Foundry; a text-only model can't read pictures. We can try it in the portal playground by attaching an image. In our app, we send one user message made of two parts: a text part with the question and an image part with the picture, given either as a public URL the service can fetch or as the file's bytes encoded in base64. We can't just pass a local file path, because the cloud can't see our disk. The model returns a plain text answer we can display. Tradeoffs: images become tokens, so big or high-detail images cost more and respond slower, and the model can misread fine print or make up details, so anything important, like a safety warning, should be checked by a person or a more precise extraction tool.
rubricPoints: The model must be a deployed, vision-capable multimodal model.
The request combines a text part and an image part in one user message.
The image is sent as a reachable URL or base64-encoded data, not a local path.
The model's output is text describing or reasoning about the image.
Names a limit such as token cost, latency, or misreading and invented details.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine sends images to a model, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about choosing the right deployment and structuring the image request adds the most.

lessons.plain: Generating images means asking an AI model to draw a brand-new picture from a written description. You type something like "a red delivery van parked at sunrise, watercolor style" and the model returns an image that did not exist before. It works a bit like briefing a fast illustrator: the clearer your brief, the closer the sketch matches what you pictured. Each request can come back slightly different, because the model invents rather than looks up. In Microsoft Foundry, you deploy an image generation model and send it text descriptions, and it sends pictures back.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you send the exact same written description to an image generation model twice, do you expect to get the exact same picture both times? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An image generation model is a generative AI model trained on huge numbers of pictures paired with captions, so it learns how words map to visual features. Given a prompt (the text description you send), it builds a new image step by step that fits that description. In Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft's platform for building AI apps, you first deploy one of these models. Deploying means creating a named, callable instance of the model inside your project. That deployment gets an endpoint, a web address your app sends requests to, and you authenticate with a key or a signed-in identity.

A request usually carries the prompt plus options: size (the pixel dimensions, such as 1024 by 1024), quality or style settings, and how many images to return. The response contains the image either as a temporary link or as base64 data, meaning the image file encoded as text.

Worked example: a marketing team wants a banner of a delivery van at sunrise. Step one, they deploy an image generation model in their Foundry project. Step two, a small client app sends the prompt "red delivery van on a quiet street at sunrise, flat illustration, no text" with size 1792 by 1024 and one image. Step three, Foundry's content filter, an automatic safety check, screens the prompt; harmful requests are blocked. Step four, the model generates the picture. Step five, the app receives the image data and saves it as a file.

A common mistake is sending the request to a chat model deployment that only interprets images. Understanding a picture and creating one are different capabilities, and you need a model built for generation. Another mistake is treating the returned link as permanent; temporary links can expire, so save the file.

In a running system, each image costs money and takes several seconds, results vary from call to call, and some prompts will be refused by the safety filter, so the app must handle refusals and slow responses gracefully.

questions.prompt: A travel blog called Hilltop Trails wants three different header pictures for a post about autumn lakes. Its developer has already deployed an image generation model in the team's Foundry project. Step A: the small client app sends the prompt "misty mountain lake in autumn, watercolor style, no people" to the deployment's endpoint, authenticating with a key, and asks for size 1024 by 1024 and three images. Step B: the content filter screens the prompt and lets it through. Step C: the model generates three pictures. Step D: the response comes back with each image given as a temporary link. Step E: ______. Step F: the blog's editor picks a favourite a week later. Which action belongs in Step E?
choices: Send the same prompt again next week, expecting to get the same three pictures back
Ask a chat model deployment to describe the links so the pictures are kept
Store the three links in the blog's database so the editor can open them next week
Download each image right away and save it as a file the blog controls
questions.why: Temporary links can expire and results vary from call to call, so the images must be saved as files straight away to still exist a week later.

questions.prompt: A startup named Pixel Kettle is setting up image generation in Microsoft Foundry. In this context, what does deploying a model mean?
choices: Training a brand-new image model from scratch on the startup's own photos
Downloading the model's files onto every customer's phone so it runs offline
Turning on the content filter so that harmful prompts are blocked
Creating a named, callable instance of the model in the project, which gets an endpoint
questions.why: Deploying creates a named, callable instance of the model inside your project, and that deployment gets an endpoint your app sends requests to.

questions.prompt: A furniture shop, Oakline, wants its app to create a new picture of a green sofa in a sunny loft. The developer sends the prompt to a chat model deployment that can look at uploaded photos and describe them, but no new picture comes back. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The image came back as base64 data, which is a format that cannot be saved
Understanding images and creating them are different capabilities, so a generation model is needed
The endpoint needed a signed-in identity because keys never work for images
The requested size of 1024 by 1024 was too small for any model to handle
questions.why: A chat model that only interprets images cannot create one; the request must go to a deployment of a model built for image generation.

questions.prompt: A greeting-card company, Sunny Post, lets customers type a description and receive a custom card picture. Which design best fits how image generation behaves in a running system?
choices: Show a clear message when the safety filter refuses a prompt, and a waiting indicator for slow responses
Assume every prompt succeeds within a fraction of a second, so no error handling is needed
Cache one result per prompt, since the same prompt always returns an identical picture
Generate unlimited extra images per request, since generating images has no cost
questions.why: Each image costs money and takes several seconds, results vary between calls, and some prompts are refused, so the app must handle refusals and slow responses gracefully.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how your app would create a new image using a model in Microsoft Foundry, and name at least one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: We deploy an image generation model in our Foundry project, which gives us an endpoint and a key or identity to call it. Our app sends a text prompt describing the picture, plus options like size and how many images we want. Foundry runs a content safety check on the prompt, the model creates a brand-new image, and the response comes back as a link or as base64-encoded data that we save to storage. It has to be a model built for generation; a chat model that only reads images will not draw one. The tradeoffs: each image costs money and takes a few seconds, the same prompt can give different results, and some prompts get refused by the filter. So we save outputs instead of relying on temporary links, show a loading state, and handle refusals with a clear message.
rubricPoints: An image generation model creates new images from a text prompt.
The model must be deployed in Foundry, giving an endpoint the client calls with credentials.
Requests include the prompt and options such as size and number of images.
The response returns image data as a link or base64 that the app should save.
Generating images differs from interpreting them, so a generation-capable model is required.
Names a tradeoff such as cost, latency, varying results, or safety-filter refusals.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine generates images, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which Foundry capability and request options fit a task builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A lightweight vision application is a small program that sends a picture to a ready-made cloud image service and gets back a description of what is in it. You do not train any model yourself. The service, called Azure Vision in Foundry Tools, already knows how to write a one-line caption, list tags such as dog or grass, find objects and where they sit in the picture, and read printed or handwritten text. Think of it like posting a photo to an expert who replies with a short written report. Your app's job is just to send the photo, say which parts of the report it wants, and use the answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your app sends a photo of a shop front to an image-analysis service, what kinds of answers would you expect back, and how might the app tell how sure the service is about each answer?
lessons.teach:
A lightweight vision app is a thin client: a small program that does no image intelligence itself and calls a hosted service over the network. In Foundry, the prebuilt image service is Azure Vision in Foundry Tools (Image Analysis). A Foundry resource is the cloud account that hosts it; it gives you an endpoint (the web address to call) and a credential (a secret key or a signed-in identity) that proves you may call it.

The client usually uses the SDK, a code library that wraps the web calls. It creates an image analysis client from the endpoint and credential, then calls analyze with two things: the image (a public URL or the raw bytes of a file) and a list of visual features, the specific analyses you want. Common features are caption (one sentence describing the scene), tags (keywords), objects (named items plus a bounding box, the rectangle coordinates where each sits), people, and read (OCR, optical character recognition, which turns text in the picture into characters). The service returns structured results, each with a confidence score from 0 to 1 showing how sure it is.

Worked example: a returns desk wants to log damaged parcels. Step 1, the app loads the photo's bytes. Step 2, it requests caption and read. Step 3, the reply contains the caption "a cardboard box with a torn corner" at 0.82 confidence and the text lines "ORDER 55120" from the label. Step 4, the app keeps only results above a threshold it chose, say 0.6, and saves the caption and order number to the record.

This works because the heavy model already exists in the cloud, so the client stays small and is cheap to change.

A common mistake is requesting every feature on every call. Each feature adds processing time and can add cost, so ask only for what the app uses. Another is hard-coding the key in source code; if it leaks, anyone can run up charges, so load it from configuration or use identity-based sign-in. In a running system, also expect throttling (calls refused when you exceed the rate limit) and handle it with a retry after a pause.

questions.prompt: A city museum builds a small app that labels photos of donated artwork for its catalogue. It needs one sentence describing each piece and any text painted on the canvas. Step 1: the app reads the Foundry resource's endpoint and key from its configuration settings and creates an image analysis client. Step 2: it takes the photo's public URL from the donation form. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the reply contains the caption "an oil painting of a harbour at sunset" at 0.91 confidence and the text line "M. KOVAC 1958". Step 5: the app keeps results above its chosen 0.7 threshold and saves both to the catalogue entry. What is Step 3?
choices: Call analyze with the URL and every available feature, so nothing is missed
Call analyze with the URL alone and let the service pick which analyses to run
Call analyze with the URL and only the caption and read features
Train a new image model on the museum's past photos before calling the service
questions.why: The app needs a scene description and the painted text, so it asks only for caption and read, which keeps processing time and cost down.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app must find each forklift in a camera photo and draw a rectangle around where it sits. Which visual feature should the app request from Azure Vision Image Analysis?
choices: Objects
Tags
Read
Caption
questions.why: The objects feature returns named items together with a bounding box, the rectangle coordinates showing where each item is in the image.

questions.prompt: A farm app asks Image Analysis for tags on a field photo. It only keeps results with a confidence score of at least 0.75. The reply contains "tractor" at 0.93, "grass" at 0.81 and "horse" at 0.42. What does the app save?
choices: All three tags, because the service returned them
Only "horse", because low scores flag unusual items
Only "tractor", because it has the highest score
"tractor" and "grass", the two at or above 0.75
questions.why: The confidence score shows how sure the service is, and the app's own threshold of 0.75 keeps only the two tags that meet it.

questions.prompt: A recycling startup's vision app sends a burst of photos to Image Analysis during a busy hour, and some calls are suddenly refused because it has exceeded the rate limit. What is the sensible way for the app to handle this?
choices: Request more visual features on each call so fewer calls are needed
Hard-code a second key in the source code and switch to it
Stop using the hosted service and run image analysis in the client
Wait a short pause and then retry the refused calls
questions.why: Refused calls from exceeding the rate limit are throttling, and the expected handling in a running system is to retry after a pause.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a small app adds image captioning and text reading using Azure Vision in Foundry Tools, what the app sends and gets back, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The app doesn't do any vision itself; it is a thin client calling the prebuilt Image Analysis service in our Foundry resource. We take the resource's endpoint and a credential, ideally an identity sign-in or a key loaded from configuration rather than written into code, and build an image analysis client with the SDK. For each picture we send either a URL or the file's bytes plus the list of visual features we need, here caption and read. The service returns a caption, the lines of text it found, and a confidence score for each, so we ignore anything below a threshold we picked. The tradeoff is that we depend on a remote service: every call adds network delay, may cost money per feature, and can be throttled, so we request only needed features and retry politely when refused.
rubricPoints: States the app is a thin client calling a prebuilt hosted image service rather than training a model.
Names the endpoint and credential needed and keeps the secret out of source code.
Says the request carries the image (URL or bytes) and a chosen list of visual features such as caption, tags, objects or read.
Explains that results come back structured with confidence scores the app can threshold.
Names a limit or tradeoff such as cost per feature, latency, throttling or dependence on a remote service.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises Foundry vision calls, so reasoning through scenarios that require picking the right service and visual features best matches how this objective is tested.

lessons.plain: Azure Content Understanding is a Foundry Tools service that reads documents and forms, such as invoices, receipts, contracts or application forms, and returns the facts you asked for as tidy, structured data. You describe the pieces of information you want, like 'vendor name' or 'total due', and the service finds them in the file and hands back named values a program can use. Think of a careful office assistant who receives a stack of paperwork and a blank checklist, fills in each line from the papers, and notes how sure they are and where on the page they found each answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a service reads a scanned invoice and returns a field called 'TotalDue = 412.50'. What else would you want the service to tell you before automatically paying that amount?
lessons.teach:
Azure Content Understanding is a managed document-analysis service. You give it a file, and it returns structured output in JSON, a plain text format of named values. It first reads the document's text and layout, meaning headings, tables and where each item sits on the page. It then uses a generative AI model to fill in the fields you asked for.

The unit you configure is an analyzer, a saved recipe that says what to pull out. Microsoft provides prebuilt analyzers for common document types, or you can build a custom one from a template. A custom analyzer holds a field schema, which is the list of fields you want. Each field has a name, a data type (string, number, date, and so on) and a plain-language description that guides the model. Each field also has a method. Extract means the value appears literally in the document. Generate means the model works the value out, such as a one-line summary. Classify means the model picks one value from a list you supply.

This works because the description tells the model what to look for, and the layout reading lets it tie each answer back to a spot on the page. For every value it returns a confidence score, which estimates how likely the value is to be right, plus grounding, which is the location in the source the value came from.

Worked example: an accounts team defines VendorName (string, extract), TotalDue (number, extract), DueDate (date, extract) and ExpenseCategory (classify: travel, utilities, office supplies). A client submits an invoice PDF to the analyzer. The service accepts the job and processes it asynchronously, meaning the client checks back later for the result. The result reads VendorName 'Northwind Power', TotalDue 412.50 at confidence 0.97, DueDate 2025-03-01, and ExpenseCategory 'utilities'. Each value points to its location on the page.

A common mistake is writing vague field descriptions, or choosing generate for a value that should be copied word for word. Another is ignoring confidence scores. In a running system, low-confidence values should go to a person for review. Otherwise wrong amounts or dates flow straight into payment and record systems.

questions.prompt:
A veterinary clinic wants to turn scanned patient intake forms into structured records with Azure Content Understanding. They build a custom analyzer, which is a saved recipe that says what to pull out of a document. Its field schema, the list of fields they want, is being filled in.

Step 1: PetName, string, method extract, because the name is written on the form.
Step 2: VisitDate, date, method extract, because the date is printed on the form.
Step 3: Species, string, method classify, with the list dog, cat, rabbit, other.
Step 4: VisitReasonSummary, string, description 'A one-sentence summary of why the owner brought the pet in, based on the notes section.' Method: ______
Step 5: A client submits a form. The service processes it asynchronously, and each returned value comes with a confidence score and a page location.

Which method completes Step 4?
choices: Classify, with a list of common visit reasons
Generate, because the model has to compose the summary itself
Extract, but change the data type to number
Extract, because the notes section is part of the document
questions.why: The one-sentence summary does not appear word for word on the form, so the model must work it out, which is what the generate method is for.

questions.prompt: In Azure Content Understanding, what is an analyzer?
choices: A saved configuration that defines what information to pull out of a document
The page location a returned value was taken from
The confidence score attached to each returned value
The JSON file the service returns after processing
questions.why: An analyzer is the configured recipe, prebuilt or custom, that tells the service which fields to extract from a document.

questions.prompt: An insurance company processes claim forms with a custom analyzer. They want a field called ClaimType that must always be exactly one of: vehicle, home or travel. The form never prints the word itself; the type has to be judged from the description of the incident. Which field method fits best?
choices: Generate, so the model writes a free-text description
Extract, so the value is copied from the page
Classify, supplying vehicle, home and travel as the allowed values
Leave the method empty and let the model decide
questions.why: Classify makes the model choose one value from a list you supply, which matches a field that must be one of three fixed options.

questions.prompt: A property firm uses Azure Content Understanding on rental agreements. The pipeline sends every returned MonthlyRent value straight into its billing system. One agreement comes back with MonthlyRent 1850 at confidence 0.38. What is the best change to the design?
choices: Switch MonthlyRent to the generate method so the model can correct itself
Delete the description for MonthlyRent so the model is not confused
Send values with low confidence scores to a person for review before they reach billing
Ignore confidence scores, since the service already found a location on the page
questions.why: A low confidence score means the value may well be wrong, so routing it to human review stops incorrect amounts from flowing into the billing system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use Content Understanding to pull key fields out of incoming forms, and name one limit or tradeoff you would design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd create a Content Understanding analyzer in Foundry, either a prebuilt one if our forms are a common type or a custom one with our own field schema. Each field gets a name, a type and a clear description. I'd mark it extract if the value is printed on the form, generate if the model must work it out, or classify if it should pick from a fixed list. Our app submits each document, waits for the asynchronous job to finish, then reads back JSON where each value carries a confidence score and grounding showing where it came from on the page. The tradeoff is that the model can be wrong, especially on poor scans or with vague descriptions. So I'd set a confidence threshold and send anything below it to a human reviewer rather than writing it straight into our finance system. That adds some manual work but prevents bad data downstream.
rubricPoints: States that an analyzer, prebuilt or custom, defines what to extract.
Describes a field schema with names, types and descriptions.
Distinguishes the extract, generate and classify methods.
Notes the output is structured JSON with confidence scores and source grounding.
Names a limit, such as possible errors, and a mitigation like human review below a confidence threshold.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises document extraction, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about analyzers, field methods and confidence handling builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Content Understanding is a Microsoft Foundry service that looks at a picture and hands back the specific facts you asked for, already sorted into labelled fields. Instead of getting a chatty paragraph about the photo, you get a tidy form filled in: colour, category, condition, a short description. Think of it like giving a clerk a blank form and a stack of photos. The clerk fills in the same boxes for every photo, so your software can read the answers without guessing. It suits jobs where many images need the same questions answered the same way, every time.
lessons.guessPrompt: An insurance company receives thousands of car-damage photos a day and wants each one to produce the same three answers: which side of the car is damaged, how severe it is, and a one-line description. Would you rather get a free-form paragraph per photo, or a fixed set of labelled answers, and why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools is a managed service that turns unstructured content, here images, into structured output that matches a shape you define. Structured output means data with named fields and predictable types, usually returned as JSON (a common text format of names and values) that code can read directly.

The central object is an analyzer: a saved configuration that says what kind of content goes in and what fields come out. Microsoft supplies some prebuilt analyzers, and you can create a custom one. A custom analyzer holds a field schema, which is the list of fields you want, each with a name, a data type (text, number, list and so on), a plain-language description, and a method. Common methods are extract (pull a value that is visibly present), classify (choose one label from a list you supply), and generate (write a value such as a summary). Behind the scenes, generative AI models read the image and use your descriptions to fill each field, which is why clear descriptions matter.

Worked example. You build an analyzer called car-damage with fields DamagedSide (classify: front, rear, left, right), Severity (classify: minor, moderate, severe) and Summary (generate, one sentence). A client app sends a photo to the analyze operation. Analysis runs asynchronously: the service accepts the request and returns an operation location, and the client polls that location until the status is succeeded. The result contains DamagedSide: front, Severity: moderate, Summary: dented bumper and cracked headlight. The app writes those three values straight into the claims database.

A common mistake is writing vague field descriptions or leaving classify fields without a fixed label list. The model then returns inconsistent wording, such as medium one time and moderate the next, and downstream code that filters or counts by severity silently miscounts. A second mistake is choosing Content Understanding when a person just wants a one-off chat answer about a single picture; a deployed multimodal model in a chat suits that better. Content Understanding earns its place when many images must yield the same reliable fields.

questions.prompt:
A supermarket chain wants every store to photograph its shelves each morning and get the same tidy data back from each photo. Structured output means named fields with predictable types, usually returned as JSON. An engineer creates a custom Content Understanding analyzer called shelf-check. An analyzer is a saved configuration describing what goes in and what fields come out. Its field schema, the list of wanted fields, contains ShelfStatus (classify: full, partly empty, empty), PriceTagText (extract the printed price) and Note (generate, one short sentence).

Step 1: The store app sends a shelf photo to the analyze operation.
Step 2: The service accepts the request and replies with an operation location, an address where the job's progress can be checked.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The app reads the result, for example ShelfStatus: partly empty, PriceTagText: 2.49, Note: top row of cereal boxes missing, and saves it to the stock database.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Poll the operation location repeatedly until the status reports succeeded, then fetch the result.
Send the same photo to the analyze operation again until the reply contains the three fields.
Read the field values directly from the reply in Step 2, because the analysis finished when the request was accepted.
Paste the photo into a chat with a deployed multimodal model and ask it to fill in the three fields.
questions.why: Content Understanding analysis runs asynchronously, so the client must keep checking the returned operation location until the status is succeeded before the structured result is available.

questions.prompt: In Azure Content Understanding, a managed service that turns images into structured output, what is an analyzer?
choices: A single JSON result returned after one image has been processed
A chat session with a multimodal model that answers questions about one picture
The address a client polls to check whether an analysis job has finished
A saved configuration that defines what kind of content goes in and which fields come out
questions.why: The analyzer is the central saved configuration; the JSON result, the operation location and a chat session are separate things.

questions.prompt: A shipping company builds a custom Content Understanding analyzer for photos of parcels. It wants two fields: TrackingNumber, which is printed clearly on each label, and PackageCondition, which must always be exactly one of intact, crushed or wet. Which methods fit these two fields?
choices: TrackingNumber: generate; PackageCondition: extract
TrackingNumber: generate; PackageCondition: classify
TrackingNumber: extract; PackageCondition: classify
TrackingNumber: classify; PackageCondition: generate
questions.why: Extract pulls a value visibly present in the image, like a printed tracking number, while classify picks one label from a fixed list you supply, like intact, crushed or wet.

questions.prompt: A hotel group uses a Content Understanding analyzer on room-inspection photos. The field RoomCondition uses the classify method, but no label list was supplied and its description just says 'condition'. Reports show values like tidy, clean and good for similar rooms, and a dashboard counting clean rooms is far too low. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Classify cannot work on photos; switch the field to the generate method.
The images are too large; resize them before sending to the analyze operation.
The vague description and missing fixed labels let the model vary its wording; add a clear description and a fixed label list.
The client read the result before polling finished; wait for the succeeded status.
questions.why: Without a fixed label list and a clear description, the model returns inconsistent wording, so code that counts by exact labels silently miscounts.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you would set up a Content Understanding analyzer instead of just sending each image to a multimodal chat model and asking about it. Explain in your own words how Content Understanding works for images and name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Content Understanding is a Foundry service that reads an image and returns structured fields I define, not free text. I create an analyzer with a field schema: each field has a name, type, description, and a method such as extract, classify against a fixed label list, or generate. My app submits an image to the analyzer, the job runs asynchronously, I poll until it succeeds, and I get JSON with the same fields every time, so I can store or filter them without parsing prose. That consistency is the reason to use it over a chat prompt when processing many images. The tradeoff is upfront design effort: if my descriptions are vague or my label lists are loose, outputs drift and downstream counts break. And for a single ad-hoc question about one picture, a multimodal chat model is simpler.
rubricPoints: States that Content Understanding turns images into structured, labelled fields rather than free text.
Explains that an analyzer with a field schema (name, type, description, method) defines the output.
Mentions methods such as extract, classify, or generate.
Notes the analyze call is asynchronous: submit, then poll for the result.
Names a tradeoff, such as schema design effort, vague descriptions causing inconsistent output, or chat being simpler for one-off questions.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises Content Understanding, and the exam skill is reasoning through scenarios to pick it over a multimodal chat prompt and design a sensible field schema.

lessons.plain: Content Understanding is a Microsoft Foundry tool that listens to a recording or watches a video and gives back neat, labelled facts instead of a raw file. You tell it what you want, such as who called, what the problem was, or a one-line summary of each scene. It returns those answers as structured data your program can store or search. Think of it as handing a long meeting recording to a careful assistant along with a form to fill in. The assistant watches it once and hands back the completed form with timestamps showing where each answer came from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team has 10,000 recorded phone calls. For each one, they want the customer's product, whether the customer was happy, and a two-sentence summary saved into a database. Would you rather get a plain transcript of every call, or a filled-in form per call? Why?
lessons.teach:
Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools is a managed extraction service. You give it a file, and it returns structured output: named fields with typed values in JSON, a common text format programs can read. It handles documents, images, audio and video. This lesson covers audio and video.

The central object is an analyzer. An analyzer is a saved configuration that says what kind of content to expect and what to pull out of it. Microsoft provides prebuilt analyzers for common jobs, such as transcribing and summarising audio or describing video. You can also build a custom analyzer by writing a field schema. A field schema is a list of fields, and each field has a name, a type (text, number, date, or a choice from a list) and a plain-language description. Each field also uses a method. Extract copies a value that is actually present, such as a stated order number. Classify picks one label from a list you supply. Generate writes a new value, such as a summary.

It works in layers. For audio, the service first transcribes the speech into text with timestamps. It also separates speakers, which is called diarization. A generative model then reads that transcript to fill in your fields. For video, it also splits the footage into segments (scenes or shots) and picks key frames, which are representative still images from each segment. It can then fill in fields for the whole video or for each segment.

Here is a worked example with a call recording. The schema has customer_product (extract), sentiment (classify: positive, neutral or negative) and summary (generate). Step 1: the client sends the audio file's location to the analyzer. Step 2: the service accepts the request and returns an operation ID, because the work runs asynchronously, meaning in the background. Step 3: the client polls, which means it checks back repeatedly until the status reads succeeded. Step 4: it reads the JSON result, for example customer_product "X200 router", sentiment "negative", plus a summary and the timed transcript.

A common mistake is to treat this as a live, real-time tool. It processes recorded files and takes time to finish. If you need instant captions while someone speaks, use a speech service instead. A second mistake is trusting generated fields as if they were quoted facts. Check them, and use descriptions that are clear and specific.

questions.prompt: A cooking school uploads a recorded 25-minute recipe video to a custom Content Understanding analyzer. It wants fields filled for each part of the video, not just the whole thing. The schema has dish_stage (classify: prep, cooking or plating), stated_temperature (extract) and chef_tip (generate). Here is how the service works through the file. First, it transcribes the chef's speech into timestamped text and separates the chef from the assistant (diarization). Second, [MISSING STEP]. Third, it picks a key frame, meaning one representative still image, from each part. Fourth, a generative model fills dish_stage, stated_temperature and chef_tip for each part and returns them as JSON. Which step is missing?
choices: It asks the client to poll for an operation ID before transcription begins
It sends the live video to a speech service so captions appear while the chef talks
It runs diarization a second time so that each speaker becomes a separate part
It splits the footage into segments, meaning scenes or shots
questions.why: Key frames are picked from each segment and the fields are filled per segment, so the service must first split the footage into scenes or shots.

questions.prompt: A law firm runs recorded witness interviews through a custom Content Understanding analyzer. In every recording, the lawyer reads the case number aloud near the start, for example "case 2291-B". Which method should the case_number field use?
choices: Extract, because the value is actually spoken in the recording and only needs to be copied
Diarization, because the case number is linked to whoever said it
Generate, because the model should write a new case number based on the conversation
Classify, because case numbers should be chosen from a list of possible labels
questions.why: Extract copies a value that is actually present, and the case number is stated outright in the audio.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit plans to host a live webinar. It wants captions to appear on screen within a second or two of each presenter speaking. A team member suggests building this with a Content Understanding analyzer. What is the best response?
choices: Build a custom analyzer with a generate field called captions so the text arrives faster
Use a speech service instead, because Content Understanding processes recorded files and takes time to finish
Use Content Understanding, but poll more often so each caption shows up sooner
Use a prebuilt audio analyzer, because prebuilt analyzers return results instantly
questions.why: Content Understanding is not a real-time tool; it works on recorded files in the background, so instant captions call for a speech service.

questions.prompt: A small app sends the location of a 40-minute recorded podcast episode to a Content Understanding analyzer. The service replies straight away with an operation ID and no fields. What should the app do next?
choices: Read the fields from the first reply, because the operation ID contains the summary
Check back repeatedly using the operation ID until the status reads succeeded, then read the JSON result
Treat the empty reply as a failure and send the same file again
Rewrite the field descriptions, because no fields came back on the first reply
questions.why: The work runs asynchronously, so the client polls with the operation ID until the job succeeds and then reads the structured output.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Content Understanding turns a recorded customer call or a training video into data a program can use. Mention one limit or tradeoff they should know before choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Content Understanding is a Foundry service that takes an audio or video file and returns structured JSON instead of just a transcript. We pick or build an analyzer, which is a saved setup with a field schema. Each field has a name, a type, a description and a method. Extract copies something actually said, classify picks from labels we list, and generate writes something new, like a summary. Under the hood it transcribes the speech with timestamps and separates the speakers. For video it also cuts the footage into segments and picks key frames. Then a model fills in our fields, either per video or per segment. Our client sends the file, gets back an operation ID, polls until the job is done, and reads the result. The tradeoff is that it works on recorded files asynchronously, so it is wrong for live captions. Generated fields can also be imperfect, so we should review them, especially when they drive decisions.
rubricPoints: Says it returns structured fields (JSON), not just raw transcripts.
Names the analyzer and field schema as the way you define what to pull out.
Distinguishes the extract, classify and generate methods.
Describes the layers: transcription with speakers and timestamps, plus segments and key frames for video.
Describes the asynchronous submit-then-poll call pattern.
Names a limit, such as not being suited to real-time use or generated values needing review.

suggested.rationale: No current mission covers media extraction, and the exam skill is choosing Content Understanding over speech or multimodal-model options in a given scenario, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Content Understanding is a Microsoft Foundry tool that reads messy files, such as scanned forms, photos, recordings or videos, and hands back neat, labelled data your program can use. You tell it which pieces of information you want, for example a vendor name and a total, and it returns those values along with how sure it is about each one. A lightweight application is a small program that sends a file to this managed extraction service and uses the answer. Think of it as a very fast clerk: you pass over a stack of paperwork and a checklist, and the clerk returns a filled-in spreadsheet with notes on anything that looked unclear.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a small app sends a 40-page scanned contract to a cloud extraction service, do you think the answer comes back instantly in the same reply, or does the app need to wait and check back later? Why?
lessons.teach:
Building a lightweight extraction app with Content Understanding means writing a small client, a program that calls a cloud service, which submits content to an analyzer and reads the structured result. An analyzer is a saved configuration that says what kind of input to expect and which fields to pull out. A field is one named piece of data, such as InvoiceTotal, with a type like number or date. You can use a prebuilt analyzer for common cases like invoices, or define a custom analyzer by writing a field schema, the list of fields and their descriptions.

The client needs three things: the endpoint, which is the web address of your Foundry resource; a credential, either an API key or a Microsoft Entra ID identity; and the analyzer ID. Analysis is a long-running operation: the service accepts the job, returns an operation reference, and the client polls, meaning it asks again every few seconds, until the status says succeeded or failed. This design exists because large documents, audio and video take time to process.

Worked example, an invoice app. Step one: choose an invoice analyzer with fields VendorName, InvoiceTotal and DueDate. Step two: the app loads the endpoint and key from environment settings, not from the source code. Step three: it submits the PDF's URL with the analyzer ID. Step four: it receives an operation reference and polls until succeeded. Step five: it reads each field's value and its confidence score, a number from 0 to 1 showing how sure the service is. Step six: InvoiceTotal comes back 1,250.00 at 0.95, so it is saved; DueDate comes back at 0.55, so the invoice is sent to a person for review.

A common mistake is treating the call as instant and reading the result straight after submitting. In a running system that produces empty or half-finished data, crashes, or silently stores blanks in a database. Always poll to completion and check confidence before trusting a value.

questions.prompt:
A car rental company, Northgate Rentals, builds a small client that pulls data from scanned damage-report forms using Content Understanding. Here is how it handles one form.

It uses a custom analyzer whose field schema lists PlateNumber (text), DamageDate (date) and RepairEstimate (number). The client reads the Foundry endpoint from environment settings and signs in with a Microsoft Entra ID identity instead of an API key. It submits the scanned form's URL together with the analyzer ID. The service returns an operation reference, and the client polls every few seconds until the status says succeeded. The client then reads each field's value and confidence score. PlateNumber comes back as KX-4471 at 0.97, so it is saved. RepairEstimate comes back as 3,800 at 0.48.

Missing step: what should the client do with RepairEstimate?
choices: Send the form to a person for review before trusting that value
Read the result again right away, because a second read will raise the score
Save it to the database, because the operation status already said succeeded
Delete the whole form's results and treat the analysis as failed
questions.why: A confidence score of 0.48 means the service is unsure, so the value should be checked by a person rather than trusted automatically, even though the operation itself succeeded.

questions.prompt: In Content Understanding, what is an analyzer?
choices: A saved configuration that says what kind of input to expect and which fields to extract
The reference the service returns so the client can check on a running job
The web address of your Foundry resource that the client sends requests to
A number from 0 to 1 showing how sure the service is about a value
questions.why: An analyzer is the saved configuration describing the expected input and the fields to pull out; the other choices describe the endpoint, a confidence score and an operation reference.

questions.prompt: A developer at a shipping firm is writing a client to extract fields from bills of lading. She has the endpoint of her Foundry resource and an API key stored in environment settings. What else does the client need before it can submit a document for analysis?
choices: A confidence score for each field
A database table to store the results
A Microsoft Entra ID identity in addition to the key
The ID of the analyzer to use
questions.why: The client needs three things: the endpoint, a credential (an API key or an Entra ID identity, not both), and the analyzer ID.

questions.prompt: A hospital's records team built a client that submits patient discharge letters to Content Understanding and reads the result on the very next line of code. Many rows in their database end up with blank fields, even though the letters contain the data. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The client used an API key instead of a Microsoft Entra ID identity
The confidence scores were below 0.5, so the service removed the values
The analyzer's field schema is too long for the service to process
The client did not poll the long-running operation until it succeeded before reading
questions.why: Analysis is a long-running operation, so reading straight after submitting returns empty or half-finished data; the client must poll until the status says succeeded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a small app uses Content Understanding to pull data out of documents, including what the app must send, how it gets the result, and one limit or tradeoff you would design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Content Understanding is a managed extraction service in Foundry. We point it at an analyzer, which is either prebuilt, like an invoice analyzer, or custom, where we write a field schema listing what we want, such as VendorName and InvoiceTotal. Our app sends the file or its URL to our resource's endpoint with a credential, ideally an Entra ID identity or a key kept in configuration, plus the analyzer ID. Analysis is long-running, so the service hands back an operation reference and we poll until it reports succeeded or failed. The result gives each field a value and a confidence score. The tradeoff is that extraction is not perfect and not instant: we must wait for big files, and we should route low-confidence fields to human review instead of saving them blindly, which adds a manual step but protects data quality.
rubricPoints: Names an analyzer, prebuilt or custom with a field schema, as what defines the fields to extract.
States the client needs the endpoint, a credential and the analyzer ID.
Explains that analysis is long-running and the client polls until it succeeds or fails.
Mentions that results include values with confidence scores.
Names a limit such as low-confidence fields needing human review or wait time for large files.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine exercises Foundry extraction, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which analyzer to use and how the client submits, polls and checks confidence adds the most.

scenarios.title: Harbourlight Home Insurance automates its claims desk
scenarios.scenario:
Harbourlight Home Insurance is a fictional mid-sized insurer. Its claims team is overwhelmed, and you have joined a small project to add AI (software that performs tasks that normally need human judgement, such as reading, listening, or deciding) to the claims process. Your lead asks you to name the right AI workload for each job and to flag the right responsible-AI concern. An AI workload is a broad category of task that AI performs, such as speech, computer vision (understanding images), text analysis, or information extraction (pulling specific, structured facts out of messy input). Responsible AI is a set of six principles for building AI that treats people well: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability.

Here is what the team has found so far. Customers mail in paper claim forms, which are scanned into images. Staff retype the policy number, the date of the incident, and the repair cost into the claims system by hand. Customers also send thousands of emails each week, and managers want to spot the angriest customers first so they can call them back quickly. A pilot model that recommends whether to approve a claim has been tested on last year's data. It turned out to recommend rejection far more often for customers in two particular postcodes, even when their claims were similar in size and type to approved claims elsewhere. Finally, the phone team records calls and wants the recordings automatically turned into written text so they can be searched later. These recordings contain customers' names, addresses, and bank details.

1. Name the AI workload that best fits turning the scanned claim forms into the three typed fields, and say briefly why it fits better than simply generating text.
2. Name the specific text analysis technique that would let managers find the angriest emails first, and explain what it outputs.
3. Name the responsible-AI principle most directly at stake with the approval model's postcode results, and describe one thing the team should do before using the model.
4. Name the speech capability needed to turn call recordings into text, and name the responsible-AI principle the team must address because of what the recordings contain.
subParts: Speech capability and its key principle
modelAnswer: Information extraction (often done with a document-reading or optical character recognition service, where optical character recognition means reading printed or handwritten characters from an image). It fits because the goal is to pull specific, known fields (policy number, incident date, repair cost) out of an image of a form and return them as structured data that can drop straight into the claims system. Trace: scanned image goes in, the service finds the text, matches it to the labelled fields, and outputs field name plus value. Generative AI creates new content, so it is the wrong tool here and risks inventing values. Accept answers that say information extraction, document intelligence, or OCR plus field extraction; a common mistake is answering simply 'computer vision' or 'generative AI' without naming extraction of structured fields.

Sentiment analysis. It reads each piece of text and scores how positive, neutral, or negative the writer's feeling is, usually as a label plus a confidence score. Managers can sort emails by the most negative scores and call those customers first. Trace: email 'Third time asking, still no reply, this is unacceptable' goes in, the output is negative with high confidence, so it moves to the top of the queue. Common mistake: choosing keyword extraction (which pulls out main topics like 'roof leak' but not feelings) or entity detection (which finds names, dates, and places).

Fairness. A fair AI system gives similar outcomes to people in similar situations and does not disadvantage groups, and postcode can act as a stand-in for things like income or ethnicity. Here similar claims got different recommendations based only on where customers live. Before use, the team should investigate and reduce the bias, for example by checking the training data for skew, testing outcomes across groups, and removing or reworking features that act as proxies; keeping a human reviewer on rejections also helps. Common mistake: answering transparency or reliability; those matter, but the core problem is unequal treatment of groups. Consequence if ignored: real customers are unfairly denied payouts and the company faces complaints and regulatory risk.

Speech recognition (also called speech-to-text), which converts spoken audio into written text; it is not speech synthesis, which goes the other way and turns text into spoken audio. The principle is privacy and security, because the recordings and transcripts hold personal and financial details that must be protected from misuse or leaks.
