Reasonable actions include collecting only what is needed, restricting who can access recordings and transcripts, protecting stored data, and masking or removing bank details from the text. Common mistake: naming speech synthesis, or naming transparency instead of privacy and security.

scenarios.title: Harborline Bikes: from chat helper to form reader
scenarios.scenario:
Harborline Bikes is a small, fictional bike-rental company with shops in three seaside towns. The two-person tech team wants AI help and has chosen Microsoft Foundry, a cloud platform from Microsoft for building AI applications. It includes a portal, which is a website where you set things up by clicking rather than writing code.

The team has three goals. First, they want a chat helper that answers customer questions about rental prices and opening hours. It must be polite and brief, and it must never invent prices. Second, they want that helper to run inside a small web page they write themselves. Third, staff fill in paper damage forms when bikes come back, and customers leave voicemails about problems. A manager wants key details such as bike ID, damage description and customer name pulled out automatically into a spreadsheet.

A model is the trained AI program that generates text. A deployment is a named, running copy of a model in your Foundry project that applications can call. A prompt is the text you send to a model. A system prompt holds standing instructions that shape every reply. A user prompt is the individual question or request.

Answer the following.

1. Explain the difference between a system prompt and a user prompt. Then write a short example of each for the Harborline chat helper. The system prompt must make the helper polite and brief and stop it from guessing prices.

2. Describe the steps to get a model ready in the Foundry portal and try it out before any code is written.

3. The team writes a lightweight chat client, meaning a small program that sends messages to the deployed model and shows the replies, using the Foundry SDK. An SDK (software development kit) is a ready-made code library for calling a service. List the pieces of information the client needs to connect. Then describe what it sends with each request.

4. Name the Foundry capability that should pull details out of the scanned damage forms and the voicemail recordings. Explain in plain terms how you tell it which details to extract.
subParts: System vs user prompt with examples
Deploy and test in the portal
Extracting details from forms and voicemails
modelAnswer:
A system prompt is a set of standing instructions the application sends with every conversation. It sets the model's role, tone, rules and limits, and the customer normally never sees it. A user prompt is the specific message for one turn, usually typed by the customer.

This split works because the model treats system instructions as background rules for every answer. Good behaviour therefore does not depend on each customer phrasing things well.

Example system prompt: "You are the Harborline Bikes assistant. Be polite and answer in no more than three sentences. Only use the prices and opening hours listed below. If a price is not listed, say you are not sure and suggest calling the shop. Never guess." The current price list and opening hours follow this instruction.

Example user prompt: "How much is an e-bike for half a day in the Westport shop?"

A common mistake is putting the rules only in the user prompt, or leaving out the price data. Then the model may invent a price, and a customer could be quoted a wrong amount.

Step 1: Sign in to the Foundry portal and open, or create, a project. A project is the workspace that holds your AI resources.

Step 2: Choose a suitable chat-capable generative model from the model catalogue, which is the list of available models.

Step 3: Deploy the model. This creates a named deployment, for example "harborline-chat", which is the running copy applications will call.

Step 4: Open the chat playground. This is a test page in the portal where you type the system prompt and user prompts and see the replies.

Step 5: Try several realistic questions, including one about a price that is not on the list. Check that the model refuses to guess, and adjust the system prompt until it behaves well.

Testing first is worthwhile because it lets you fix the prompts before writing any code. A common mistake is skipping this testing, which means prompt problems are only discovered after customers start using the helper.

To connect, the client needs three things. The first is the endpoint, which is the web address of the Foundry project or resource. The second is a credential that proves the app may call the service, such as a key or a signed-in identity. The third is the deployment name, for example "harborline-chat", which tells the service which running model to use.

With each request, the client sends a list of messages, each tagged with a role. There is one system message containing the system prompt, then the user message. For a multi-turn conversation, the earlier user and assistant messages are also included so the model has the context. The client then reads the model's reply from the response and shows it on the page.

A common mistake is using the original model's name instead of the deployment name, or forgetting to resend the system message. The first causes failed calls. The second makes the helper lose its rules, for example by starting to guess prices.

Use Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools. It is a managed information-extraction service: you give it files and it returns structured fields, meaning named pieces of data, instead of raw text. One service handles documents and forms, images, and audio and video, so it covers both the scanned forms and the voicemails.

You tell it what to extract by setting up an analyzer, which is a reusable definition of the fields you want. For damage forms, the fields might be bike ID, date, damage description and staff name. For voicemails, they might be customer name, bike ID and problem description. The service works through the content, transcribing speech in the case of audio, and fills in those fields.

A lightweight client can then send each new file to the analyzer and write the returned fields into the spreadsheet. A common mistake is choosing a plain chat model or a basic text-reading tool and then hand-parsing its output. That approach is less reliable and produces inconsistent spreadsheet rows.
